items.title: Quantum Many-Body Scars from Operator Size
items.summary: We present a general construction of approximate many-body scar states in two copies of a system using a bilocal size interaction that couples one site to its partner on the other copy. For an uncoupled two-sided Hamiltonian whose terms have fixed size in an operator basis, we identify polynomially many Krylov basis states that it annihilates and that, in the thermodynamic limit, become concentrated on a single size sector. The size operator splits them into a tower of equally spaced levels that gives rise to coherent revivals characterized by collective oscillations of energy across the two copies. We provide a concrete realization of this construction in two copies of a general $q$-body nearest-neighbor spin chain, and the SYK model.
items.author: Debarghya Chakraborty, Dario Rosa

items.title: Nonperturbative Bounds on the Ground-State Energy of Lattice QED
items.summary: We establish nonperturbative bounds on the ground-state energy of lattice quantum electrodynamics with naive fermions in Coulomb gauge, within the Gaussian photon approximation. Our central result is a spectral comparison theorem showing that, in the thermodynamic limit, the minimum fermionic energy density over all link configurations coincides with that of the trivial gauge configuration. The proof exploits a logarithmic determinant representation and dimensional reduction, without relying on reflection positivity, and applies to lattices of either parity. Combining this result with the positivity of the electromagnetic and Coulomb Hamiltonians, we derive an explicit lower bound on the interacting ground-state energy. Finite-lattice counterexamples show that the thermodynamic limit is essential.
items.author: Paweł Zin, Andrzej Veitia

items.title: Localization of weakly integral objects in braided fusion categories
items.summary: An object $X$ of a braided fusion category is called weakly integral if $\mathrm{FPdim}(X)^2$ is an integer. We prove that every nonzero weakly integral object admits a localization, that is, a Yang-Baxter operator $R$ on a finite-dimensional vector space $W$ such that, for every $n$, the algebra homomorphisms from the group algebra of the braid group $B_n$ to $\mathrm{End}(W^{\otimes n})$ and to $\mathrm{End}(X^{\otimes n})$, defined by $R$ and by the braiding, have the same kernel. The operator $R$ can be chosen unitary when the braided fusion category is unitary. This proves the 'if' direction of a conjecture of Rowell and Wang, motivated by topological quantum computation, which states that a simple object admits a localization if and only if it is weakly integral. For a simple weakly integral object of a unitary braided fusion category, the operator $R$ that we construct has an enhancement in the sense of Turaev, and the resulting knot invariant is the Reshetikhin-Turaev invariant of knots colored by $X$.
items.author: César Galindo

items.title: A Microwave-Photonics Formulation of the Rydberg-Atom Receiver
items.summary: The performance of Rydberg-atom receivers is seldom stated as a radio-frequency (RF) link budget. The receiver is shown to be an intensity-modulated direct-detection analog optical link whose modulator is the laser-driven vapor. The transmission of a warm vapor is derived in closed form by averaging the four-level response over atomic velocities. The conversion gain, noise figure, bandwidth, intercept points, and spurious-free dynamic range follow from this one function. For a weak probe the instantaneous bandwidth is half the width of the transparency window in two-photon detuning. The local-oscillator beat places the second-order intercept near twice the local-oscillator field, so the local oscillator sets the even-order linearity. For a rubidium transition at 17.04 GHz the closed forms agree with a velocity-resolved density-matrix model to 1% for the slope and the intercepts and to 10% for the bandwidth. They underestimate the group delay by a third. The response is tied to atomic constants, and the sensing volume escapes the Chu limit. However, the noise figure of a warm vapor rules it out as a general replacement for an antenna and low-noise amplifier.
items.author: David Rosser

items.title: Transpilation-Aware Multi-Vendor QPU Scheduling with Predicted Post-Transpilation Fidelity
items.summary: Cluster schedulers already choose nodes, GPUs and accelerators for submitted workloads, enforce quotas and spread load. QPUs from several vendors are now schedulable resources in the same clusters, yet the user still names the device, usually the one with the best average fidelity. For a given circuit that choice is often wrong: compiling onto each device's qubit connectivity adds gates, so a job can meet its required success probability on one device and miss it on another with similar error rates, and checking this exactly by compiling for every candidate is too slow for a scheduling decision. We let the scheduler choose the QPU in two stages. A training-free estimate predicts, in milliseconds and without compiling, the success probability on every candidate and filters out those that would miss the requirement; only the chosen device then compiles the circuit, re-checks it, and binds the job or rolls back. The estimate matches compiling every candidate at about 25x lower latency in simulation, ranks measured success on IBM hardware as well as the post-compilation estimate (Spearman rho = 0.95), reduces requirement violations from tens of jobs to a few, and avoids them under contention without piling jobs onto one device. Across vendors it works when error rates are comparable (IBM and IQM) and fails when published figures overstate a device.
items.author: Ana Paula Appel

items.title: The moments and asymptotic spectral distribution of the Grassmannian ensemble
items.summary: In this paper, we study random density matrices constructed by taking partial traces of projections onto random subspaces of a bipartite Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_{B}$ distributed according to the pushforward measure of the action of the unitary group on the Grassmannian $\text{Gr}_{n}(\mathcal{H}_A \otimes \mathcal{H}_{B})$. This ensemble models a `typical' quantum subspace. All tracial moments of the density operator, as well as mixed tracial moments of reduced density operators, are computed explicitly using Weingarten calculus. There are several consequences of these results. In particular, we prove that the empirical spectral distribution of the density operator converges almost surely to a rescaled Marchenko-Pastur law. We also prove that this ensemble can be written as a sum of asymptotically free random density operators, leading to an alternative proof of the convergence of the spectral distribution. Finally, we compute the asymptotic expansion of the average entanglement entropy.
items.author: Aryan Gadhave, Asghar Ghorbanpour, Liam Hickey, Masoud Khalkhali et al.

items.title: Metadata-Private Voice Communication over Tor using Post-Quantum Key Encapsulation
items.summary: Encrypted voice communication systems commonly protect call content but expose significant metadata, including the network identities of both parties, call timing, and traffic patterns. Simultaneously, advances in quantum computing threaten the asymmetric primitives underlying conventional key exchange, creating a harvest-now, decrypt-later risk for long-lived sensitive communications. Existing systems address at most one of these concerns: secure VoIP applications such as Signal and Wire rely on centralized infrastructure and classical cryptography, while anonymous communication tools built on the Tor network support only text messaging and lack post-quantum key encapsulation. This paper presents SAPEC (Secure Anonymous Peer Exchange Communicator), a peer-to-peer voice communication system that simultaneously addresses anonymity, decentralization, and quantum resistance. SAPEC routes all traffic exclusively through Tor hidden services, concealing the IP addresses of both parties, and augments the standard TLS handshake with a custom protocol layer that performs ML-KEM-1024 key establishment, a settle on AES-256 symmetrical keys and mutual Dilithium identity verification before any audio is transmitted. All audio is subsequently encrypted under AES-256. A removable Crypto Ignition Key prevents identity key material from being stored on the device. Empirical evaluation across 45 independently circuit-rebuilt test runs yielded a median one-way audio delay of 355 milliseconds and a median connection setup time of 7.61 seconds on same-region Tor circuits, demonstrating that interactive voice communication over onion routing is practically achievable.
items.author: Noah Zeinali Yazdi, Samuel Zeinali Yazdi

items.title: Optimised 8th-Order Trotter-Suzuki Schemes for Quantum Simulation
items.summary: Simulating quantum dynamics in many-body systems is one of the most promising applications of quantum computers. Product formulas are a natural choice for this task, since they map directly onto quantum gates, and increasing their order $n$ could lead to reduced gate depths, provided the parameters are chosen efficiently. So far, schemes beyond $6^{\textrm{th}}$ order have only been built as compositions of second-order schemes, while more general product formulas are known only up to $6^{\textrm{th}}$ order. In this work, we extend our optimisation framework to order $n = 8$, and find both more efficient compositions and the first $8^{\textrm{th}}$ order general schemes. Our formulas improve on the theoretical efficiency of the state-of-the-art schemes by Morales et al and we recommend two schemes explicitly. In simulations of the Heisenberg XZ chain one of our recommended schemes always outperforms those by Morales et al, though it is not always the same scheme that performs best. More generally, we observe that for Hamiltonians split into many non-commuting operators the uniformity of a Trotter decomposition becomes the main indicator of a scheme's performance. To assess the schemes' use on quantum hardware, we simulate noisy circuits with our new Qiskit plugin qiskit-omelyan. At current noise levels, the Leapfrog scheme remains the best choice, but as noise rates decrease toward fault tolerance, our recommended schemes become competitive.
items.author: Marko Maležič, Johann Ostmeyer

items.title: Thermo-electric Response Bound on Fluctuations in Coherent Transport
items.summary: We establish an accessible lower bound on current noise in coherent electron transport, expressed in terms of responses to reservoir temperatures and chemical potentials. Derived within the Floquet-Nambu scattering formalism using a Cramér-Rao-type inequality, it holds for arbitrary linear combinations of charge and heat currents in normal terminals, including those of hybrid superconducting systems, under static or periodic driving. The bound is tight in experimentally relevant regimes, notably in quantum point contacts with static or oscillating voltages and normal-superconductor junctions, often providing stronger constraints than thermodynamic uncertainty relations. It can be evaluated via experimentally accessible response coefficients, without inferring entropy production or dynamical activity, and provides useful constraints on the precision of nanoscale thermal and quantum devices.
items.author: Gianmichele Blasi, Rosa López, Mykhailo Moskalets, Sungguen Ryu

items.title: Quantum Dobrushin comparison and locality of fermionic equilibrium states
items.summary: We prove a quantum analogue of Dobrushin's comparison theorem for lattice fermions. As in the classical case, it is a tool for proving uniqueness of equilibrium states, decay of correlations, and stability of local expectations under distant perturbations. We apply it to fermions with weak many-body interactions added to a quadratic Hamiltonian, allowing pairing, spatial inhomogeneity and long-range interactions. If the quadratic Hamiltonian is gapped, there is a coupling strength below which the thermal equilibrium (KMS) state is unique at every positive temperature and its correlations decay uniformly in the temperature. Its local expectations converge to those of the unique gapped ground state exponentially fast in the inverse temperature. In the same regime, local perturbations perturb locally in a strong sense (strong LPPL): every equilibrium state of a system with a distant defect is locally close to the equilibrium state without the defect, however strong or extended the defect is. The same holds for finite-volume Gibbs states with arbitrary even boundary terms. Without a gap, uniqueness, decay of correlations and strong LPPL hold at each positive temperature for interactions below a coupling strength that depends on the temperature. At high temperature, they hold for general interactions.
items.author: Lennart Becker, Harman Preet Singh, Stefan Teufel

items.title: World Models for Learning Quantum Many-Body Dynamics
items.summary: We propose using world models for learning Hamiltonians from measured dynamics of a quantum computer or simulator. Implicitly, the parameters of a Hamiltonian are encoded in how the measured few-body observables evolve. By using a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) to perform prediction in latent space, we show that the device Hamiltonian can be efficiently inferred from noisy measurements. We train a spatiotemporal encoder and predictor with approximately $2.7$ million trainable weights using a single objective, to predict the representation of the next window of measurements from the previous one. The network is thereby driven to retain the reproducible dynamics and discard shot noise. We recover the field and coupling maps of a two-dimensional Ising lattice in real and imaginary time, and the disorder map of a one-dimensional Heisenberg chain of $100$ sites. In every settings the encoder achieves lower error than a masked autoencoder and than the same encoder left untrained. It also outperforms the same regression head applied directly to time-averaged observables, by factors of $4.4$ to $30$. We establish latent prediction as a practical self-supervised objective for learning from measurements of quantum dynamics.
items.author: Yuan Wang, Oleksandr Kyriienko

items.title: Tackling Many-Body Coulomb Singularity by Randomization
items.summary: Many-body Coulomb dynamics is central to quantum chemistry and molecular simulation, yet the Coulomb singularity undermines both the standard error analysis and performance of product formulas. Even for the simple hydrogen ground state, the celebrated Trotter formulas converge more slowly than their nominal order, and going to higher order does not help. Randomization by itself does not resolve this. We show that conventional qDRIFT suffers the same loss of accuracy, and that for general initial states, the errors of both Trotter formulas and qDRIFT can decrease more slowly than any power of the number of time steps (logarithmically). To overcome these limitations, we introduce supersmoothing qDRIFT, a randomized product formula that turns a physical property of free particle propagation into an algorithmic resource. Our algorithm achieves an error bound that decreases linearly with the time step, uniformly over \textit{all} initial states and without any smoothness or energy assumptions. Combined with spatial discretization analysis, the resulting end-to-end gate count improves on those of qubitization and high-order Trotter formulas applied directly to the discretized Hamiltonian, despite first-order convergence in time. This work demonstrates new ways of utilizing continuum dynamics to achieve algorithmic advantage.
items.author: Di Fang, Wook Yoon

items.title: Compilation-informed probabilistic logical-error cancellation
items.summary: The potential of quantum computers to outperform classical ones in practically useful tasks remains challenging in the near term due to scaling limitations and high error rates of current quantum hardware. While quantum error correction (QEC) offers a clear path towards fault tolerance, overcoming the scalability issues will take time. Early applications will likely rely on QEC combined with quantum error mitigation (QEM). We introduce a QEM scheme against both compilation errors and logical-gate noise that is circuit-, QEC code-, and compiler-agnostic. The scheme builds on quasi-probability methods and uses information about the circuit’s gates’ compilations to attain an unbiased estimation of noiseless expectation values incurring a constant sample-complexity overhead. Moreover, it features maximal circuit size and code distance both independent of the target precision, in contrast to strategies based on QEC alone. We formulate the mitigation procedure as a linear program, demonstrate its efficacy through numerical simulations, and illustrate it for estimating the Jones polynomials of knots. Our method significantly reduces quantum resource requirements for high-precision estimations, offering a practical route towards fault-tolerant quantum computation with precision-independent overheads for fixed circuit size and code distance.
items.author: Giancarlo Camilo, Thiago O. Maciel, Allan Tosta, Abdulla Alhajri et al.

items.title: Interferometry radii at RHIC BES energies within the integrated HydroKinetic model
items.author: V. Yu. Naboka, Yuri Sinyukov, M. D. Adzhymambetov, H. Zbroszczyk

items.title: The role of entropy production and thermodynamic uncertainty relations in the asymmetric thermalization of open quantum systems
items.summary: The asymmetry between heating and cooling in open quantum systems is a hallmark of nonequilibrium dynamics. Here, we investigate the thermalization of a quantum system weakly coupled to a bosonic thermal bath under detailed balance, focusing on the entropy production rate and the quantum thermokinetic uncertainty relation (TKUR). Within the sector of states that remain diagonal in the energy basis we derive a perturbative expression for the time-dependent entropy production rate by expanding the relative entropy around equilibrium in terms of Liouvillian eigenmodes. Through this expansion, we determine that the spectral gap, the overlap of the initial state with the slowest decay mode, and the mode weight control the entropy production. Particularly for the thermal qubit, the ratio of the initial rates of heating and cooling has an exact closed form. Heating involves a higher initial entropy production, and hence faster thermalization, solely because of its larger spectral gap, i.e., the bath-temperature dependence of the dissipative rate. The TKUR is then used as a diagnostic tool that relates the asymmetry to the precision bounds on heat-current fluctuations. The analysis presented here is intended to clarify the thermodynamic origin of the asymmetry within the well-controlled Markovian case.
items.author: A. Tejero

items.title: Nanosculpting in Superconducting Fe(Te,Se)/Bi2Te3 with Focused Si++ Ions and Implications on Vortex Pinning
items.summary: We demonstrate “nanosculpting” of ∼150 nm-wide focused ion beam (FIB)-irradiated channels into thin films of FeTe0.75Se0.25/Bi2Te3 (FTS/BT), a candidate topological superconductor, with a Si++ FIB. Systematic irradiation shows that increasing the ion dose, while keeping the beam energy constant, progressively suppresses both the critical temperature (Tc) and threshold current (I*) (the current at which the voltage reaches 20 mV), confirming the creation of a nanoregion with “degraded” superconductivity. Kelvin probe force microscopy, atomic force microscopy, and scanning electron microscopy corroborate the structural and electronic modification of the irradiated region. I* (B) measurements reveal a slower field-induced decay of I* at higher doses. These results are consistent with the irradiation-induced enhanced vortex pinning. Based on these observations, we discuss the next steps as future work toward the fabrication of lateral topological-Josephson Junctions based on FTS/BT, which can be a foundation for the development of robust and scalable fault-tolerant qubits.
items.author: Debarghya Mallick, Sujoy Ghosh, An‐Hsi Chen, Qiangsheng Lu et al.

items.title: Quantum chaos diagnostics for non-Hermitian systems from bi-Lanczos Krylov dynamics
items.summary: In Hermitian systems, Krylov complexity has emerged as a powerful diagnostic of quantum dynamics, capable of distinguishing chaotic from integrable phases, in agreement with established probes such as spectral statistics and out-of-time-order correlators. By contrast, its role in non-Hermitian settings, relevant for modeling open quantum systems, remains less understood due to the challenges posed by complex eigenvalues and the limitations of standard approaches based on orthogonality, such as singular value decomposition. Here, we demonstrate that Krylov complexity, computed via the bi-Lanczos algorithm, provides a reliable probe of quantum chaos in non-Hermitian systems, clearly discriminating chaotic and integrable regimes. Our results agree with complex spectral statistics and complex spacing ratios, underscoring the robustness of the method. Universality is supported by extensive tests in the non-Hermitian Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model and random-matrix ensembles across multiple non-Hermitian symmetry classes, with further validation provided by the non-Hermitian random-field XXZ model as a pseudo-Hermitian system.
items.author: Matteo Baggioli, Kyoung-Bum Huh, Hyun-Sik Jeong, Xuhao Jiang et al.

items.title: Tracking Large Chemical Reaction Networks and Rare Events by Neural Networks
items.summary: Chemical reaction networks are widely used to model stochastic dynamics in biophysical processes. Their exact probabilistic description via the chemical master equation becomes intractable for high-dimensional systems due to the exponential growth of the state space. This difficulty is further exacerbated when metastable transitions and rare events dominate the dynamics. Here, we present an advanced neural-network approach that effectively tackles large reaction networks and rare-event dynamics within a unified framework. Building on autoregressive representations of the full joint probability distribution, we achieve efficient training through second-order optimization methods, including natural gradient descent and the time-dependent variational principle. We leverage enhanced-sampling strategies that enable accurate resolution of low-probability regions governing rare transitions. We demonstrate the method on a multistable genetic toggle switch and a mitogen-activated protein kinase cascade consisting of 16 species and 35 reactions with dense coupling. We further quantify rare events in spatially extended Schlögl models in both one- and two-dimensional lattices, reaching system sizes with extremely large state spaces up to 3 × 10 15 . These results highlight the potential of neural modeling as a flexible and scalable framework for studying high-dimensional chemical reaction networks and rare events.
items.author: Jiayu Weng, Xinyi Zhu, Jing Liu, Linyuan Lü et al.

items.title: High-temperature Gibbs states are uniformly Markovian and trivial
items.summary: We prove that, above a constant temperature threshold, Gibbs states of local noncommuting qudit Hamiltonians exhibit exponential decay of mutual information and conditional mutual information (CMI). Specifically, we prove exponential decay of the CMI for arbitrary spatial tripartitions $A \sqcup B \sqcup C$ which need not comprise the entire system, thereby establishing a \textit{uniform Markov property} for high-temperature Gibbs states. A central obstruction to proving such bounds is that conventional cluster expansions for the logarithm of reduced Gibbs states can fail to converge due to noncommutativity. Our main insight is to construct a classical representation of the Gibbs state using an overcomplete basis. Although such representations generally involve negative quasiprobability weights, we show that a decomposition based on projective 2-designs admits a convergent cluster expansion with strictly positive weights at sufficiently high temperatures, allowing us to circumvent the obstruction. The separability of high-temperature Gibbs states is a natural byproduct of this decomposition. Finally, in the context of mixed-state phases of matter, our results imply that high-temperature Gibbs states belong to the same mixed-state phase as the maximally mixed state.
items.author: Andrew D. Kim, Tai Hsuan Yang, Jong Yeon Lee

items.title: Local velocimetry for atomic superfluids: from Riemann rarefaction waves to quantized vortices
items.summary: We demonstrate local velocimetry for atomic superfluids in two dimensions (2D). Using matter-wave interferometry based on Raman--Bragg beam splitters, we map the local gradient of the phase of the superfluid's wavefunction onto displacement of the interference fringes and reconstruct the 2D velocity field. We illustrate the capabilities of this technique by applying it to two canonical problems. First, we directly observe the self-similar evolution of the velocity field in 1D Riemann rarefaction flows. Second, we map out the full 2D velocity field around quantized vortices, explicitly demonstrating the quantization of velocity circulation.
items.author: Yansheng Zhang, Yi Jiang, Feiyang Wang, Louis Depaepe et al.

items.title: Query-Optimal Quantum Minimum Finding from Numerical Estimators
items.summary: We propose a quantum minimum-finding algorithm for objectives accessed via numerical estimators that avoids the logarithmic query overhead of amplifying the confidence of estimates before the search. A coherent estimator that is $\varepsilon$-accurate with probability at least $2/3$ on each of $N$ labels suffices to find a $2\varepsilon$-optimal label using $O(\sqrt N)$ base-estimator queries at constant confidence. The query bound and the additive-error constant are separately worst-case optimal. More generally, suppose a preparation assigns probability mass at least a known $p$ to objective values at most $a$. Without knowing $a$ or the prepared distribution, our algorithm returns a candidate and an estimate $v$ such that, jointly with constant probability, $v$ is $\varepsilon$-accurate for the candidate and $v\le a+\varepsilon$. The algorithm uses $O(p^{-1/2})$ queries to each of the preparation and estimator oracles in the worst case, and the selected candidate can be retained as a quantum state. For preparation width $s_P$ and estimator workspace width $w$, it requires $O(s_P+w+\log\log(4/p))$ qubits, independently of the requested confidence. Applications give worst-case optimal $Θ(\sqrt N/η)$ queries for selecting an $η$-optimal bounded expectation, and guided ground-energy estimation using $O(ω^{-1})$ preparations and $O((ωη)^{-1})$ elementary controlled-evolution queries at constant confidence, where $ω$ is a lower bound on the guiding state's ground-space amplitude overlap.
items.author: Egil Bae

items.title: Fast, in-place, and ancilla-free quantum algorithms for integer multiplication and inversion
items.summary: Arithmetic operations are a fundamental building block in the design of quantum algorithms, with their implementation cost expected to have a significant impact on the viability of a wide variety of quantum applications. In this work, we present novel algorithms for a number of in-place quantum arithmetic operations that are highly efficient in terms of their space and gate count overheads compared to the current state-of-the-art. We show that in-place modular multiplication of integers, modulo a power of two, can be performed with either a classical or quantum odd multiplier using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates and no ancilla qubits, for any $ε>0$. We then show that standard in-place integer multiplication can be performed with a non-zero classical or quantum multiplier using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates for any $ε>0$, with no ancilla qubits required for the classical multiplier and a logarithmic number of ancilla qubits for the quantum. Using our quantum modular multiplication algorithm, we also show that in-place modular inversion, modulo a power of two, can be performed using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates and no ancilla qubits, for any $ε>0$. To our knowledge, these are the first quantum algorithms achieving both subquadratic gate counts and sublinear ancilla counts for each of the considered in-place operations. All but one of these fast operations are optimal in terms of memory, only requiring enough space to store the output of the operation, which overwrites the input directly. We present our multiplication algorithms as consequences of a single unified theorem, which may find further application within quantum arithmetic.
items.author: David Halpenny, Adithya Sireesh, Petros Wallden

items.title: Scalable Simulation of Strongly Correlated Fermions with Neural Gaussian Tensor Networks
items.summary: Accurate simulations of strongly correlated electrons remain a central challenge in computational physics. We introduce neural-network Gaussian projected entangled-pair states (NN-GPEPS), which exploit the locally-entangled subspace of Gaussian states to give an architecture more compatible with modern neural networks and an exact contraction cost of $O(N^{3/2})$ on two-dimensional lattices. For the Hubbard model at $U/t=8$ and $1/8$ hole doping, we obtain state-of-the-art variational energies in large lattices of up to 1024 sites. These results demonstrate an accurate approach to strongly correlated fermions by connecting neural networks with Gaussian tensor networks.
items.author: Runze Chi, Ao Chen, Garnet Kin-Lic Chan

items.title: High-Accuracy Neural-Network Quantum States via Randomized Real-Time Dynamics
items.summary: Neural-network quantum states (NQSs) exhibit a disparity in converging to the ground state during energy minimization: while the energy converges quadratically with the error in the variational wave function, other observables converge only linearly, which limits the accuracy of physical predictions. Here we show how to close this gap by introducing a new algorithm that improves the accuracy of NQSs. Our method, termed dynamical averaging, estimates expectation values by averaging over a state (or observable) evolved in real-time. Using insights from quantum information, we prove an up-to-quadratic suppression of error in arbitrary ground state observables, thus matching the fast convergence of the energy. Importantly, this improved accuracy requires neither further energy minimization nor increased model complexity, but rather exploits the effect of randomization on quantum states. We demonstrate dynamical averaging on non-integrable spin models, where it accelerates convergence and substantially reduces errors in observables.
items.author: John M. Martyn, Rod Rofougaran, Samuel Stein, Di Luo

items.title: End-to-End Quantum Algorithm for Differential Equations: Application to Simulating a Biomolecular System
items.summary: Quantum algorithms for differential equations have the potential for substantial algorithmic speedups over classical methods. However, they rely on certain assumptions and abstract oracle specifications that leave their practical feasibility and computational advantages for realistic applications unclear. Here we formalize the concept of an end-to-end quantum algorithm for differential equations as one that accepts classical inputs and returns classical outputs, and provide implementations for algorithmic primitives in constructing such algorithms. We present a tailored end-to-end quantum algorithm for the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann (LPB) equation, a partial differential equation (PDE) with variable coefficients widely used in simulating a biomolecular system. We explicitly implement all aspects of the algorithm, from preparing an initial state to generating a quantum solution and estimating properties of the system. In particular, we develop a new discrete representation for variable-coefficient PDEs on a grid that enables efficient implementation of the operator oracle, and build on a recent technique based on optimal wavelet preconditioning to generate a quantum solution with a cost independent of the condition number of the discretized operator. We show the algorithm can be implemented by quantum circuits of size polylogarithmic in both the number of grid points $N_g$ and the inverse of the desired accuracy $\varepsilon$, with an overall gate cost polylogarithmic in $N_g$ and quasilinear in $1/\varepsilon$. We also show the classical preprocessing to construct the circuits has polylogarithmic cost in $N_g$ and $1/\varepsilon$. Our work provides a concrete end-to-end quantum algorithm for a PDE of practical value, demonstrates an exponential improvement in scaling
items.author: Mohsen Bagherimehrab, Daniyaal Farooqi, Gavin K. Brennen, Barry C. Sanders et al.

items.title: Classically Trained Quantum Generative Models with Shared Training and Fine Tuning for Quantum Matter
items.summary: Ground-state measurement statistics characterize quantum matter. Selected correlations can guide the classical training of a quantum sampler even when sampling the full distribution is difficult. We ask whether training across related ground-state distributions helps the sampler reproduce their correlations more accurately. We train a hypernetwork to map Hamiltonian parameters to circuit angles, sharing information across the phase diagram before local fine-tuning with additional reference data for quantum deployment. For classical training, we derive an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of Fourier coefficients for circuits built from general Pauli rotations, with a cost that depends on the circuit generators. We also introduce a CDF-KL loss for comparing selected marginals. We study the Haldane Hamiltonian and transverse-field Ising model, using an automated search to select reference calculations near phase transitions. On the twelve-site chain, the adaptively pretrained hypernetwork matches the independent fits' final mean total variation distance in fewer local updates and continues to a lower error. On a 1,024-site chain and a 4 by 256 lattice, the fine-tuned circuits have lower squared maximum mean discrepancy from the reference distributions than the independent circuits at the evaluated point in each geometry. These results motivate shared training for preparing quantum samplers across a phase diagram and local fine-tuning.
items.author: Mario Herrero-Gonzalez, Elham Kashefi, Mina Doosti

items.title: Classical Oracle Separation of QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy and Quantum Cryptography Even When P = QCMA
items.summary: Remark: This work is in submission at STOC'27 and thus the full manuscript has been publicly posted on the conference website since November 3rd, 2026. Inspired by the Codeword-Hash Structure problem recently introduced by Cakan (arXiV, 2026) to separate $\mathsf{QMA}$ from $\mathsf{QCIP}$, we introduce a new problem called Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise ($\mathsf{CHN}$) and prove that, in the query complexity model, it is in $\mathsf{QMA}$ but hard for the $\mathsf{QCMA}$ hierarchy $\mathsf{QCMAH} = \bigcup_{d\geq1}\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathsf{QCMA}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{QCMA}}}}$, the classical-witness quantum-verifier analogue of $\mathsf{PH}=\bigcup_{d\ge1}\mathsf{NP}^{\mathsf{NP}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{NP}}}}$. Using this problem, we show that there exists a classical oracle ${O}$ such that $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O} =\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O} \subset \mathsf{QMA}^{O} \text{ but } \mathsf{QMA}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O},$ thus showing that quantum state or quantum proof advantage could exist even if classical computers can efficiently solve any problem that can be quantumly verified with a classical proof. Further, using our problem, we show that various quantum cryptographic primitives can exist even when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{QCMA}$ and thus neither quantum-computable one-way functions nor (verifiable) quantum computational advantage exist. In particular, relative to a classical oracle ${O}$ with $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O}$, there exist pseudorandom states with classical keys and public-key encryption with copy-protected quantum decryption keys and classical public keys and ciphertexts, among other primitives, answering an open question of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal (STOC 2025).
items.author: Alper Cakan

items.title: Authenticating quantum key distribution through random position checks
items.summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) requires some form of authentication in order for the parties to be sure they are not unknowingly generating a key with an adversary pretending to be one of the honest parties. In this work, we propose a protocol in which the position of one of the parties is used as the authentication credential for key distribution. Our protocol essentially consists of a BB84 QKD protocol with quantum position verification (QPV) rounds randomly interleaved in. The approach is efficient compared with previous approaches, which required running an entire QPV protocol for every bit requiring authentication. We undertake an initial security analysis of the protocol for a restricted set of attacks.
items.author: Florian J. Curchod, Erik Woodhead, Cameron Foreman, Marcel Mordarski et al.

items.title: On the design of sequential quantum repeaters with error detection
items.summary: Long-distance, trust-free quantum communications rely on the development of scalable quantum repeater schemes. Sequential entanglement generation with error detection is a promising approach that combines manageable implementation requirements with a hop-by-hop architecture compatible with existing classical infrastructure. In this paper, we investigate key design choices for such schemes over a repeater chain using quantum key distribution as a benchmark. We find that simple quantum error-detecting codes, such as repetition codes or quantum parity codes, perform well under near-term hardware assumptions and outperform strategies without any encoding. In particular, we show that two-qubit repetition codes may well be all that we need to implement in many practical scenarios. We also examine different architectures for the generation of initial entanglement and assess their merits. Additionally, we show that moderate improvements in some hardware components can partially mitigate the slow technological progress of others.
items.author: Javier Rey-Domínguez, Koji Azuma, Mohsen Razavi

items.title: Hamiltonian Stabilization of the Two-Photon Dicke Model
items.summary: Collective two-photon light--matter interactions enable pair amplification but can destroy spectral confinement, preventing a stable thermodynamic bright phase. We show that a positive Kac-scaled number-Kerr interaction renders the two-photon Dicke Hamiltonian of \(N\) emitters lower-bounded at all couplings while preserving its generalized \(\mathbb Z_4\) symmetry. We determine the exact zero-temperature thermodynamic energy density with \(O(N^{-1})\) finite-size control and obtain the global phase diagram. A bright minimum is born at a saddle-node and exchanges global stability with the normal minimum at coexistence, producing a discontinuous photon-density jump. Symmetry-resolved exact diagonalization through \(N=128\) supports the predicted density jump and an exponentially closing same-sector normal--bright tunneling gap. Spectral collapse thus becomes the singular zero-Kerr point of a first-order phase diagram, identifying a Hamiltonian route to stabilizing pair amplification.
items.author: Pradip Laha, Kingshuk Adhikary, Subhashish Banerjee, Peter van Loock

items.title: Residual Allan Stability under Periodic Auxiliary Ramsey Sampling
items.summary: The timing of auxiliary Ramsey measurements can change the frequency stability associated with a drifting pulse shift at a fixed nominal Fisher-information rate for a constant shift. For periodic instantaneous observations of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck shift with causal prediction between updates, we derive the exact residual covariance averaged over the update cycle and the corresponding Allan variance at arbitrary averaging times. Relative to a continuous Kalman reference at the same information rate, periodic estimation increases the cycle-averaged estimation-error variance, reduces the short-time residual Allan variance, and increases its long-time value. Its covariance decays more slowly at the origin and has a larger integral. We extend the result to instantaneous sensing of the sum of finitely many independent Ornstein-Uhlenbeck modes. Integrated observations preserve the short-time ordering for the scalar shift, and numerical calculations resolve the dependence of the crossover on window duration. A zero-order-hold comparison shows that the short-time ordering can change when the same estimator drives a different correction command. A three-level Ramsey model of coherent population trapping (CPT) maps the discriminator response to an effective information budget and illustrates how the dark times affect the choice of schedule.
items.author: Zhiqian Su

items.title: A Nonsecular Quantum Master Equation with Detailed Balance and Second-order Error Bound
items.summary: An effective theory of open quantum systems should preserve the detailed balance structure inherited from microscopic reversibility and remain accurate throughout relaxation. Meeting both requirements is particularly challenging in quantum many-body systems, where dense spectra can invalidate the secular approximation even at weak coupling. Here we construct a nonsecular quantum master equation that satisfies time-reversal Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (TR-KMS) detailed balance. Under suitable conditions, we prove a time-uniform $O(λ^2)$ bound on the difference between the predicted and exact reduced density matrices, where $λ$ is the system-bath coupling strength. Our construction completes the Redfield generator by imposing detailed balance while matching its dissipative and coherent coefficients at resonance. In this approach, TR-KMS detailed balance is compatible with resonance matching, whereas its counterpart without time reversal is not. In a benchmark against the exact microscopic dynamics of two coupled oscillators, our equation maintains $O(λ^2)$ accuracy across secular and nonsecular regimes, outperforming the existing detailed-balance equations tested. These results provide a systematic route from microscopic models to thermodynamically consistent descriptions of open quantum dynamics beyond the secular approximation.
items.author: Ji-Hui Pei, Jin-Fu Chen

items.title: Dressed-State Quantum Information Processing Using a Multilayer Ion Trap Chip with an Integrated Radio Frequency Resonator
items.summary: We present the experimental preparation of a radio frequency (RF)-dressed-state qubit, the coherent operation of a single RF-dressed qubit, and the selective readout of RF-dressed hyperfine states of $^{171}$Yb${^+}$ ions trapped using a novel microstructured ion trap chip. We demonstrate the individual addressing of RF-dressed-state qubits in a two-ion Coulomb crystal. To this end, we developed, manufactured, and characterized a trap chip specifcally designed for quantum information processing with RF-dressed-state qubits. The chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated resonator that creates a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude along the axis of a linear ion crystal. This RF gradient enables the individual addressing of dressed qubit states as well as their coupling. We characterize the ion trap chip experimentally using the hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of laser cooled $^{171}$Yb${^+}$ ions and by applying a single, global, modulated RF field oscillating near 12.6 GHz that drives dressed-state resonances. We present a microfabricated multilayer ion trap chip specifically designed for quantum information processing based on dressed-state qubits. This ion trap chip consists of multiple layers, one of which includes an integrated radio frequency (RF) resonator, creating a gradient of the RF magnetic field amplitude that allows for individual qubit addressing and qubit-qubit coupling. We experimentally characterize this ion trap chip demonstrating dressed-qubit state preparation, coherent single dressed-qubit operation, and dressed-state-selective read-out using hyperfine states of the electronic ground state of $^{171}$Yb${^+}$. For this purpose, a global modulated RF driving field oscillating near 12.6 GHz is applied
items.author: Ivan A. Boldin, Elham Esteki, Bogdan Okhrimenko, Friederike Giebel et al.

items.title: Residual-Algebraic Design of Symmetry-Preserving Variational Quantum Circuits
items.summary: Symmetry-preserving (SP) variational quantum circuits restrict evolution to physically relevant sectors of Hilbert space, but symmetry preservation alone does not guarantee accessibility within those sectors. We show that a restricted generator set can possess a residual dynamical Lie algebra whose commutant further decomposes the target symmetry sector into invariant blocks. The associated block populations are conserved and impose a kinematic upper bound on the fidelity with a target state. We then invert this diagnostic into a circuit-design principle: candidate SP generators can be screened before variational optimization by asking whether they break the residual commutant, which invariant blocks they couple, and what adjoint module they generate under the residual algebra. For two orthogonal residual blocks we prove that a single elementary real inter-block rotation generates the full orthogonal algebra. We further derive a complex escape criterion: if the real and imaginary parts of an inter-block seed are independent over the residual intertwiner algebra, the generated module is the full complex coupling space and the enlarged algebra becomes special unitary. A connected residual-block graph yields a natural multi-block generalization and suggests minimum-cost spanning-tree circuit design. We demonstrate this design principle in the XXZ and Hubbard models, where residual-algebra screening identifies SP circuit extensions that remove the relevant accessibility obstructions. These examples establish a unified route from residual-symmetry diagnosis and fidelity bounds to predictive quantum circuit design.
items.author: Sahinur Reja

items.title: CREST: A Hardware-Aware GNN-Based Framework for High-Fidelity and Robust Superconducting Quantum Compilation
items.summary: Quantum compilation on superconducting processors requires selecting a connected execution region whose topology and calibrated properties suit the input circuit. This choice constrains subsequent routing and influences the noise encountered during execution, yet aggregate hardware-quality metrics alone may not reliably predict the execution fidelity of a given circuit. Calibration updates can also change region suitability and trigger the rebuilding of calibration-dependent resource structures. We present CREST, a graph neural network (GNN)-based framework that evaluates circuit-region compatibility before routing. It encodes gate dependencies and logical-qubit interactions alongside each candidate region's connectivity and current calibration attributes; bidirectional cross-graph attention relates the two representations, while real-device execution outcomes supervise candidate ranking. The trained scorer is reused with updated calibration attributes. Evaluations on 324 circuits from seven datasets on TianYan-176 show that CREST improves mean measurement-distribution fidelity by 19.03% over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest mean fidelity on every dataset. Furthermore, using updated calibration attributes, the same trained model maintains the highest overall mean fidelity across six measurement dates without retraining. With a unified model of circuit-region compatibility, CREST improves execution fidelity across diverse workloads and sustains that advantage as hardware calibration changes.
items.author: Wenjie Sun, Xiaoyu Li, Zhigang Wang, Yuchen He et al.

items.title: Quantum Simulation of First-Quantised Chemistry with a Sum-of-Squares Representation
items.summary: Calculating molecular energies is expected to be an important application of quantum computers, but the most efficient algorithms to achieve this typically have significant space requirements. Scaling quantum processors to thousands of logical qubits is a daunting engineering challenge, so developing algorithms that run with reduced qubit requirements is of particular importance. Moreover, most algorithms are benchmarked on active spaces with about as many orbitals as electrons, missing dynamical correlation which is necessary to describe real chemistry. Capturing this correlation requires several times more orbitals than electrons, even in compact atomic-orbital basis sets. This low-filling regime favours first quantisation, where each electron is represented by a number of qubits that grows only logarithmically with the number of orbitals. Whether this approach translates into a practical advantage in orbital basis sets of realistic size, however, has been unclear. Here, we develop a first-quantised phase estimation algorithm for generic orbital basis sets, based on a non-convex sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian and spectral-gap amplification. We compare it with the state-of-the-art second-quantised algorithm, compiling both with the same techniques at the logical level. For six molecules with 4 to 24 electrons in 5 to 14 times as many orbitals, our first-quantised method needs up to 16 times fewer Toffoli gates than the second-quantised algorithm in the low-qubit regime, where only a few hundred logical qubits are available. It stays cheaper up to between several hundred and about 1\,400 qubits, and its smallest qubit count is 1.4 to 2 times lower than in second quantisation. items.author: Aleksei V. Ivanov, Christoph Sünderhauf, Jon Kunjummen, Nick S. Blunt et al.

items.title: Hurst Exponent Estimation with Quantum Wavelets
items.summary: How accurately can the Hurst exponent $H$ of fractional Brownian motion be estimated from repeated preparations of a single amplitude-encoded path, when every measurement interrogates the same realization? We extend the $ε$-decimated quantum nondecimated wavelet transform in three directions: we remove the endpoint jump of circular filtering, derive the sampling distribution of the estimator, and compare readouts at equal query budgets. A one-qubit mirror extension removes the jump and keeps every coefficient that straddles a fold of the same order as an interior coefficient, for any compactly supported filter and circular shift. The transform for any such filter is compiled from the paraunitary lattice of its filter bank, and the energy share of a level is the success probability of one multiply-controlled reflection, which is both the controlled unitary of a Hadamard test and the oracle of amplitude estimation. For filters with at least two vanishing moments we prove a root-$N$ central limit theorem for the log-energy contrasts, independent of the limiting path norm, so the studentized estimator is asymptotically standard normal for deterministic query budgets under which the success count at every level diverges. For sparse counts we give a working multinomial--lognormal likelihood, exact in its readout model for direct measurement, and check its coverage by simulation. For paths of length $512$, mirroring reduces RMSE by a factor of $3$--$10$ for $H\ge0.5$, and with exact shares the nondecimated db2 estimator is $6$--$14\%$ above the root Cramér--Rao bound. Hadamard level tests are less accurate than direct measurement of the leading qubits at every budget. At $H=0.9$ and $2^{20}$ queries, maximum-likelihood amplitude estimation attains RMSE $0.0347$, against $0.045
items.author: Brani Vidakovic

items.title: The limits of inertia bounds on graph powers
items.summary: We investigate the tightness of inertia and inertia-type bounds related to graph powers. This class of graphs appears in several contexts, such as the theory of distance-regular graphs, quantum information theory and coding theory. They are a priori not covered by previous separation constructions involving locally sparse graphs, see Kwan and Wigderson (2024), or Alon's pseudorandom graphs, see Elphick, Tang and Zhang (2025). Instead, we apply the latter's lower bound for complements of pseudorandom graphs to random graphs and random Cayley graph constructions, whose graph-power structure is ensured by additive combinatorial arguments. From this we are able to conclude that also for graph powers there can be a large gap between inertia bounds and the actual independence number. For the inertia-type bound, which is based on polynomials, we achieve even larger separation by considering sequences of graphs whose spectrum converges to a continuous distribution. Our methods draw from several areas of mathematics, ranging from additive combinatorics and probabilistic methods, to character sums over finite fields and arithmetic geometry.
items.author: Aida Abiad, Nils Van de Berg, Sam Mattheus

items.title: Time-Varying Medium from an Ensemble of Laser-Dressed Quantum Emitters
items.summary: We propose a minimal quantum-mechanical model of a frequency dispersive, time-modulated medium that explicitly incorporates the pumping mechanism. It consists of a homogeneous ensemble of quantum emitters dressed by a pump laser. We analyze their dispersive, time-varying response to a perturbative probe field by deriving the macroscopic polarizability of the ensemble, and then solving Maxwell's equations via the Floquet formalism. This yields a rich band structure that departs from conventional analyses in which the modulation source is neglected, arising from the interplay between the dispersive polaritonic and time-varying responses. These results shed light on the role of the modulation source in time-varying media and pave the way toward realizing dispersive time-varying media from driven quantum-mechanical systems.
items.author: Adrián Juan-Delgado, Diego Martín-Cano, Paloma A. Huidobro

items.title: The limits of magic-state cultivation
items.summary: Fault tolerance is understood through Pauli algebra, which fails at non-Clifford gates. Circuits such as magic-state cultivation, which checks an encoded T state with physical T gates, have therefore lacked an exact theory of which faults are harmful. We develop such a theory and show that, for any circuit that prepares a magic state with non-Clifford gates and postselection, one stabilizer code on the non-Clifford gates decides which faults are harmful. This ties cultivation to distillation, bounds its T-count from below and gives an exact test. For a single check on an ideally encoded state, the fault distance reduces to Pauli algebra on the code. As a use case, we analyze the S gates that have stood in for T gates in the design of cultivation. We show that this proxy can only overstate the fault distance of such a check, and that the checks in use, on color and surface codes, tolerate at most half as many faults as their code allows. The theory also yields nearest-neighbor checks that keep the full distance, certified up to code distance nine.
items.author: Llorenç Balada Gaggioli, Jakub Mareček

items.title: Shedding Light on Quantum Non-Classicality: Witnessing Wigner Negativity with Free Electrons
items.summary: Certifying quantum non-classicality like Wigner negativity typically demands full optical state tomography. This work introduces a noise-resilient framework for witnessing optical Wigner negativity using phase-resolved quantum photon-induced near-field electron microscopy (QPINEM). By mapping electron coherences directly to symmetrically ordered optical characteristic functions within a coupling-limited phase-space region, the protocol bypasses full optical reconstruction. A post-measurement witness matrix is constructed via Bochner's theorem from recorded electron spectra, where negative eigenvalues certify non-classicality. To ensure reliability under realistic experimental conditions, a noise-aware selection procedure decouples discovery from statistical validation. Benchmarked across various optical preparations-including vacuum-Fock superpositions, odd cat states, and GKP states-the protocol provides a statistically bounded pathway for probing quantum features with free electrons.
items.author: Sunjun Hwang, Leong Chuan Kwek

items.title: Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning
items.summary: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has attracted increasing interest as a possible route to construct feature representations that are difficult to reproduce with classical models. However, near-term QML architectures based on trainable parametrized quantum circuits remain affected by limited hardware resources, noise, and severe optimization difficulties such as barren plateaus. In this work we propose Soft-MoQE, a Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts architecture that replaces variational quantum training with the input-dependent selection and combination of fixed quantum feature maps. The model is composed of a heterogeneous pool of non-trainable quantum circuits, each defining a distinct embedding, and a classical gating network that learns how to weight these embeddings for each data point. We benchmark Soft-MoQE on three PCA-reduced tasks: MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST. Soft-MoQE outperforms the single best expert, the uniform average of all experts and a linear baseline, achieving task-dependent performance comparable to that of a trainable quantum neural network, without optimizing any quantum parameter and with a quantum training cost that is lower by orders of magnitude. The analysis of the class- conditioned expert usage shows that the learned routing combines a few experts for each input, with a selection that depends on the class. These results support the learned routing among fixed quantum circuits as a trainability-aware design principle for hybrid QML.
items.author: Valeria Repetto, Romina D'Aurizio, Piero Farinelli

items.title: Mathematical artificial data for operator learning
items.author: Wu Heng, Benzhuo Lu

items.title: Multi-fidelity predictive model for shock response of energetic materials using conditional U-Net
items.summary: Mapping microstructure to properties is central to materials science. Perhaps most famously, the Hall-Petch relationship relates average grain size to strength. More challenging has been deriving relationships for properties that depend on subtle microstructural features and not average properties. One such example is the initiation of energetic materials under dynamical loading, dominated by energy localization on microstructural features such as pores, cracks, and interfaces. We propose a conditional convolutional neural network to predict the shock-induced temperature field as a function of shock strength, for a wide range of microstructures, and obtained via two different simulation methods. The proposed model, denoted MISTnet2, significantly extends prior work that was limited to a single shock strength, model, and type of microstructure. MISTnet2 can contribute to bridging atomistics with coarse-grain simulations and enable first principles predictions of detonation initiation and safety of this class of materials.
items.author: Brian H. Lee, Chunyu Li, Aidan D. Pantoya, James P. Larentzos et al.

items.title: Bandedge-State-Limited Single-Photon Emission from Volumetric Quantum Design of 2D Colloidal Quantum Wells
items.summary: Abstract Present-day solution-processable single-photon sources are dominated by three-dimensionally confined colloidal quantum emitters, yet their particle-to-particle variation in single-exciton properties limits reproducibility and scalability. Here, to avoid such heterogeneity, we demonstrate reliable room-temperature single-photon emission from atomically flat two-dimensional (2D) colloidal quantum wells (CQWs) with inherently uniform one-dimensional quantum confinement, despite their long-standing limitations of efficient multiexciton emission and pronounced exciton-surface susceptibility. We resolve these challenges through volumetric quantum design (VQD) of CQWs, yielding a highly localized, single bandedge state. This design laterally confines the bandedge excitonic domain within the exciton coherent area and vertically decouples it from surface states via a thick, strain-relieved quantum-barrier shell that preserves strong confinement, overcoming the daunting thickness-confinement trade-off in 2D CQWs. Statistical single-particle spectroscopy reveals that VQD-CQWs deliver near-blinking-free (on-time: >99.5%) and fluence-insensitive antibunching (g(2)(0): ∼0.041), protected by a bandedge-state-filling bottleneck, together with linear polarization of up to 73% under cavity-free conditions, originating from synergistic transition-dipole and electric-field anisotropies. These advances establish 2D CQWs as a viable, homogeneous and scalable platform for quantum technologies.
items.source: Journal of the American Chemical Society
items.author: Xiao Liang, Bo Wang, Yue Yu, Pedro Ludwig Hernández‐Martínez et al.

items.title: Expressivity of two-dimensional Gaussian fermion tensor network states
items.summary: Tensor network states (TNS) provide a family of efficiently compressed approximations to physically relevant many-body quantum states. An important quantity that characterizes the computational resources required by a TNS is its bond dimension. While in one dimension an area law for the Renyi-0 entropy guarantees an exact matrix product state representation with a bond dimension independent of the system size, an analogous statement does not hold for general states in two dimensions (2D). This leaves open the question of how the expressivity of 2D TNS is related to the entanglement properties of the states they represent. In this work, we focus on two families of 2D translation-invariant Gaussian fermionic states: single-band BCS superconductors and half-filled two-band insulators (including semimetals). For each family, we prove that an area law for the Renyi-0 entropy is equivalent to having an exact Gaussian fermionic TNS representation with a finite bond dimension determined by the Renyi-0 entropy. We also establish equivalent characterizations in terms of compactly supported Wannier-type orbitals and the momentum-space wavefunction, relating the spatial extent of these orbitals and the structure of the wavefunction to the required bond dimension.
items.author: Pok Man Tam, William Musk, Zhehao Dai

items.title: From nonlocal correlations to local symmetry breaking: Asymmetry dynamics of crosscap states
items.summary: Under unitary dynamics preserving a global symmetry, bipartite entanglement typically grows while an initially broken symmetry is locally restored. Here, we show that this conventional scenario can be reversed when symmetry-breaking coherence is initially encoded in long-range entanglement. We investigate this phenomenon in a family of charge deformed crosscap states, characterized by antipodal entangled pairs with tunable entanglement and symmetry breaking. We first characterize their static properties, finding a Page-like entanglement profile and an entanglement asymmetry that vanishes for subsystems smaller than half the system size, but grows logarithmically for larger subsystems. For symmetric subsystems, we also analyze the symmetry-resolved entanglement and investigate how it evolves as the subsystem is continuously deformed away from a symmetric partition. Following a quench to a free-fermion tight-binding chain, we uncover an unconventional dynamics in which the entanglement entropy decreases whereas the entanglement asymmetry increases, so that initially symmetric subsystems dynamically develop local symmetry breaking. This behavior is quantitatively captured by a quasiparticle picture describing the propagation of antipodal correlations. Our results reveal how symmetry-preserving dynamics can redistribute globally encoded symmetry-breaking coherence, making it locally accessible, and establish the initial entanglement structure as a key ingredient in determining the fate of local symmetries out of equilibrium.
items.author: Konstantinos Chalas, Pasquale Calabrese, Colin Rylands

items.title: Modeling quantum information scrambling in realistic protein NMR experiments
items.summary: Out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) are important probes of operator spreading and information scrambling, and have recently been proposed as a means of extracting molecular structural information through nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). Realizing this potential requires accurate modeling of OTOCs in complex molecular environments within experimentally relevant settings. Here, we develop an end-to-end computational pipeline connecting molecular structures to OTOC dynamics in protein systems. Our framework incorporates molecular motion through molecular dynamics simulations, orientational averaging appropriate for powder samples, and spin-network truncation, using an experimentally realizable double-quantum effective Hamiltonian. We apply this framework to a dataset of over 350 carbon-carbon spin pairs across 10 protein systems, spanning interspin distances of 5-17 A. We find that OTOC arrival times scale approximately linearly with interspin distance, revealing system-dependent operator-spreading velocities that enable correlations to propagate over extended distances within milliseconds. Our sensitivity analysis further shows that individual OTOCs predominantly constrain a single structural parameter, primarily associated with interspin distance. Together, these findings highlight the potential of OTOCs to probe spatially extended spin correlations on timescales compatible with solid-state NMR experiments.
items.author: Alec F. White, Joseph Haslehurst, Daniel R. Moberg, Justin Provazza et al.

items.title: Local interference algorithms for observables in large random circuits
items.summary: In quantum dynamics, it is generally believed that interference effects lead to a sign problem for classical Monte Carlo sampling methods, rendering sampling ineffective. In this paper we show that this is generically not the case for the task of simulating the evolution of observables in random instances of circuit dynamics. Specifically, we consider two examples of observables which give large signals despite the randomness of the dynamics: first order out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) in unstructured random circuits without conservation laws and time-ordered charge-charge correlators (TOCs) in particle number-preserving random circuits. We show that these observables can be approximated by classical stochastic processes and that these approximations can be systematically improved with a series expansion that incorporates coherent corrections associated with clusters of gates. We design and implement algorithms that combine Monte Carlo sampling and tensor network methods to approximate the series. We observe numerically that the computational complexity of approximating TOCs and OTOCs scales polynomially in the circuit size and in the target precision. We study the accuracy of these algorithms by directly mapping their ensemble-averaged errors to partition functions of replica statistical models, allowing for perturbative analysis and numerics in $1$d brickwork geometries. Our theoretical analysis explains the empirical observation of polynomial complexity of these algorithms and is consistent with polynomial complexity extending to arbitrarily small precision and to the thermodynamic limit.
items.author: Philippe Suchsland, Brayden Ware, Vladislav D. Kurilovich, Vadim Smelyanskiy et al.

items.title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime
items.summary: Ensemble prediction of nonlinear dynamics propagates a probability density whose linear transport equation retains the nonlinear drift, but grid-dependent circuit costs leave end-to-end feasibility in early fault-tolerant quantum computing unresolved. We couple polynomial reduced-order models fitted by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics to Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann (KvN) transport and surface-code resource estimation. At fixed model dimension and drift degree, per-step transport rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with cells per reduced coordinate. Balancing model accuracy against circuit costs makes reduced-model polynomial degree a design variable for early fault-tolerant quantum simulation. For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, preparation, propagation and sampling to 1% relative root-mean-square field error against the radial model are estimated to take 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits. Estimated three-coordinate wake runtimes span hours to weeks below one million qubits. IBM hardware experiments demonstrate nonlinear radial KvN transport for this wake, using reference circuits to mitigate noise.
items.author: Hansol Noh, Unam Oh, Sangkyu Baek, Doyeol et al.

items.title: Performance analysis of a Rydberg atom THz radiometer concept
items.summary: THz receiver technology lies between electronics and photonics; as such, its implementation is not as mature. This warrants investigation into alternative THz receivers such as Rydberg atom sensors, which are highly susceptible to electric fields. In particular, the conversion architecture has been demonstrated to coherently transduce thermal radiation. This system offers room-temperature operation and does not necessarily require a local oscillator at the frequency of the input signal. We provide an assessment of the feasibility of such sensors for THz radiometry within the context of Earth observation.
items.author: Richard J. Murchie, Petronilo Martin-Iglesias, Julian Hofmann, Christophe Buisset

items.title: Quantum amplification with a linear quantum coupler
items.summary: Josephson parametric amplifiers (JPAs) are essential components for quantum-limited microwave measurement, but their dynamic range is often constrained by Kerr and other pump-induced nonlinear effects. In this work, we systematically study the performance of a parametric amplifier based on the linear inductive coupler (LINC). Starting from the driven-circuit Hamiltonian, we derive the effective three-wave-mixing amplifier model, including leading flux-driven nonlinear corrections relevant to realistic operation. We analyze the resulting gain response, saturation behavior, and intermodulation distortion, comparing them with representative state-of-the-art JPA designs. Our results show that the symmetry-protected structure of the LINC suppresses static Kerr nonlinearity. Moreover, suitable circuit-parameter optimization can further reduce the dressed-squeezing and driven-Kerr effects, leading to considerable improvements in power-handling metrics. These results identify the LINC architecture as a promising platform for high-linearity Josephson parametric amplification.
items.author: Changqing Wang, Yao Lu

items.title: Integral Tensor Isomorphism via Cubic Rings and Lattice Methods
items.summary: We prove that isomorphism of integral $2\times3\times3$ tensors under $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ is decidable in bounded-error quantum polynomial time. For a tensor $T=(A,B)$ with nonzero determinant form $\det(xA-yB)$, we use the parametrization of Wood by balanced modules to reduce the isomorphism problem to principality tests for compatible lattices, and use the algorithms of Bley, Hofmann, and Johnston to solve this in BQP. When the determinant form vanishes identically, we get either an integral $2\times2\times2$ core, or a polynomial kernel vector of degree one or two. The linear-kernel case yields another compatible lattice problem, while the quadratic-kernel case reduces to a fixed system of polynomial congruences and unimodular lifting. A quantifier-elimination argument decides these congruences in deterministic polynomial time given the prime factorization of the modulus, which quantum integer factorization supplies. Finally, we show that zero padding preserves integral $2\times2\times2$ tensor isomorphism, yielding a polynomial-time reduction from real-quadratic principality to the identically singular $2\times3\times3$ problem.
items.author: Thomas Huffstutler

items.title: Teleportation of Logical Qubits using Lattice Surgery with Superconducting Circuits
items.summary: Demonstrating a quantum advantage when solving large-scale computational problems on a quantum computer requires the correction of errors that occur due to limitations in control accuracy and coherence. Using the concept of quantum error correction, fault-tolerant logical qubits can be realized and manipulated with logical single- and two-qubit gates. In this paper, we experimentally analyze fault-tolerant lattice-surgery, which is a key primitive that enables operations between logical qubits realized in the surface-code. Using this primitive, we demonstrate the teleportation of logical states between two distance-three logical qubits realized in a superconducting circuit composed of 41 physical qubits. Throughout this process, we study the step-by-step transfer of logical information from a source to a target logical qubit by characterizing the time evolution of logical observables. We find that repeated execution of stabilizer measurements, after merging two surface-code patches, restores fault tolerance and yields increased fidelity of the teleported state. When optimizing the protocol in terms of gate count and sequence duration, we observe further improvements in fidelity. Our work offers new insights into the optimization of fault-tolerant lattice-surgery operations, while also providing a comprehensive description of the physical device and gate sequences used. We expect the efficient implementation of increasingly complex logical circuits to enhance the performance of future fault-tolerant quantum computers.
items.author: Luca Hofele, Yongxin Song, Áron Márton, Ian Hesner et al.

items.title: Quantum simulation of neutral-meson mixing and decay on a reprogrammable photonic processor
items.summary: Neutral mesons oscillate into their antiparticles while decaying, so their dynamics is generated by a non-Hermitian effective Hamiltonian which a quantum simulator restricted to unitary operations cannot implement directly. We propose a reprogrammable photonic processor that simulates this open-system evolution through dilation and analyze it at the circuit level. The effective Hamiltonian is reconstructed exactly from measured lifetimes, mass and width differences, and the CP-violation parameter $|q/p|$. Through a singular-value decomposition and a single ancilla that encodes the total decay probability, its propagator is embedded in a four-mode unitary, which is compiled at each time step into a rectangular interferometer on a hexagonal mesh of tunable Mach-Zehnder units. Circuit simulations including coupler, propagation, and bend losses show that one fixed device, reprogrammed only through its control voltages, reproduces the flavor oscillation and decay of neutral kaons and of $B_d$ and $B_s$ mesons, with $x=Δm/Γ$ from 0.77 to 26.9. Over 500 time steps per system, the mean fidelity lies between 0.99979 and 0.99982, and no step falls below 0.9996. Because every optical path crosses nine tunable units, uniform insertion loss reduces only the transmitted power, whereas unit-to-unit loss variations lower the fidelity quadratically, $1-\langle F\rangle \simeq 0.08σ^2$ for a loss standard deviation $σ$ in dB. A leading-order analysis traces this coefficient to the routing of light through the mesh, reproduces the fitted value to within 2%, and explains why it is the same for all three mesons; a mean fidelity of 0.999 tolerates $σ\approx 0.11$ dB. The ancillary outputs encode the total decay probability without postselection, and the reported probabilities are normalized
items.author: Mohd Abu Bakar Siddique, Abrar Al Shadid Abir, A. K. M. Rakib, Mohammad Abrar Kabir et al.

items.title: Non-equilibrium topological order from Floquet anyon proliferation in the toric code
items.summary: We analyze the dynamics of Kitaev's toric code in Floquet quenches where the drive coherently creates and propagates fermionic $f$ anyons. We show that the long-time state departs from pure-state topological order but retains long-range entanglement, thereby realizing a Floquet analog of intrinsic mixed-state topological order. As a key result enabling this analysis, we derive decompositions of the entanglement entropy and logarithmic negativity that separate the ground-state value, including topological terms, from a contribution given by the driven quasiparticles. For a drive inducing non-interacting $f$ dynamics, these decompositions allow us to leverage numerical methods for free fermions and to link the emergence of the proposed long-time ordered state to the equilibration of $f$ anyons to a periodic Gibbs ensemble. For drives inducing Floquet eigenstate thermalization of $f$, our results suggest a scenario where Floquet heating of the $f$ sector stabilizes a genuine non-equilibrium topological phase, in contrast with the usual view of heating as an obstacle to order in periodically driven systems.
items.author: Francesco Petiziol

items.title: Causality, determinism and predictability: Probing nature through classical and quantum eyes
items.summary: In this article, mainly focussed on students and interested readers, we discuss how the understanding of causality, determinism and predictability is transformed as we move from the classical world view to the quantum description. We first explain how determinism and predictability operate in classical dynamics and outline the notion of causality. A paradigm shift occurs within the framework of quantum mechanics where we have to revisit, and even give up, the notions of determinism, predictability and maybe even strict causality. An engrossing and fascinating debate ensues, after the formulation of quantum mechanics among the giants of physics like Einstein, Bohr, Heisenberg, Pauli, and many others. While some questions have been settled in the last century in favour of quantum world view, there are still many open questions, most important of which is the role of gravity in shaping events within the quantum framework.
