items.source: Indian Journal of Pure and Applied Mathematics
items.author: Hoang-Son Tran, V. Petrovic, Rémi Bardenet, Subhroshekhar Ghosh

items.title: Spectral diffusion of phosphorous donors in silicon at high magnetic field
items.summary: We study the central spin physics of a phosphorus donor electron in silicon interacting with a silicon-29 bath at high magnetic field (8.59 T). We find that the spectral diffusion time is shorter and exhibits a larger anisotropy with respect to crystal orientation in the magnetic field than in previous measurements at 0.35 T. The increased anisotropy suggests a modification of the hyperfine interactions at high field. The 1.2 THz cyclotron energy is a significant fraction of the 10.8 THz Rydberg energy of the bound donor, which can result in a non-trivial magnetic perturbation of the hydrogenic donor wavefunction. Low-power, above-bandgap optical excitation is seen to increase the spectral diffusion time, recovering the low-field spectral diffusion time at most crystal orientations. Understanding such perturbations to the spatial wavefunction of donor electron spins could be key to engineering their high-fidelity control.
items.author: Ethan Q. Williams, Lihuang Zhu, J. van Tol, Chandrasekhar Ramanathan

items.title: Holographic covering and the fortuity of black holes
items.summary: We propose a classification of BPS states in holographic CFTs into monotone and fortuitous, based on their behaviors in the large N N limit. Intuitively, monotone BPS states form infinite sequences with increasing rank N N , while fortuitous ones exist within finite ranges of consecutive ranks. A precise definition is formulated using supercharge cohomology. We conjecture that under the AdS/CFT correspondence, monotone BPS states are dual to smooth horizonless geometries, and fortuitous ones are responsible for typical black hole microstates and give dominant contributions to the entropy. We present supporting evidence for our conjectures in the {\cal N}=4 SYM and symmetric product orbifolds.
items.author: Chi‐Ming Chang, Ying-Hsuan Lin

items.title: Experimental decoherence mitigation using a weak measurement-based scheme and the duality quantum algorithm
items.summary: Abstract We experimentally demonstrate a weak measurement and measurement reversal-based scheme to ameliorate the effects of decoherence due to amplitude damping, on an NMR quantum processor. The weak measurement and measurement reversal processes require the implementation of non-unitary operations, which are typically infeasible on conventional quantum processors, where only unitary quantum operations are allowed. We employed the duality quantum algorithm (DQA) for experimentally realizing the amplitude damping channel and non-unitary quantum operations corresponding to weak measurement and measurement reversal. We experimentally validate the efficacy of the weak measurement-based decoherence mitigation scheme by showing state protection on a four-qubit system, with one qubit being designated as the ‘system qubit’, while the remaining three qubits serve as ‘ancilla qubits’. Our experimental results clearly demonstrate the success of the weak measurement-based decoherence mitigation scheme in protecting the desired state. Since the measurement process involved has trace less than unity, the scheme can be thought of as a filtration scheme, where a subset of the spins is protected while the rest of the spins can be discarded.
items.author: Gayatri Singh, Akshay Vijay Gaikwad, Arvind, Kavita Dorai

items.title: Partition function estimation with a quantum coin toss
items.summary: Abstract Estimating quantum partition functions is a critical task in a variety of fields. However, the problem is classically intractable in general due to the exponential scaling of the Hamiltonian dimension N in the number of particles. This paper introduces a quantum algorithm for estimating the partition function $Z_\beta$ of a generic Hamiltonian $H$ up to multiplicative error based on a quantum coin toss. The coin is defined by the probability of applying the quantum imaginary-time evolution propagator $f_\beta[H]=e^{-\beta H/{2}}$ at inverse temperature $\beta$ to the maximally mixed state, realized by a block-encoding of $f_\beta[H]$ into a unitary quantum circuit followed by a post-selection measurement. Our algorithm does not use costly subroutines such as quantum phase estimation or amplitude amplification; and the binary nature of the coin allows us to invoke tools from Bernoulli-process analysis to prove a runtime scaling as $\mathcal{O}(N/{Z_\beta})$, quadratically better than previous general-purpose algorithms using similar quantum resources. Moreover, since the coin is defined by a single observable, the method lends itself well to quantum error mitigation. We test the resulting coin-estimation protocol in practice with a proof-of-concept 9-qubit experiment using variationally compiled block-encodings. Our findings offer an interesting alternative for quantum partition function estimation relevant to early-fault quantum hardware.
items.author: Thais de Lima Silva, Lucas Borges, Leandro Aolita

items.title: Deriving Tsallis entropy from q-deformed Hamiltonian within a statistical mechanics framework
items.author: Paradon Krisut, Sikarin Yoo-Kong

items.title: A near-quantum-limited diamond maser amplifier operating at millikelvin temperatures
items.summary: Abstract Current microwave quantum technologies require the amplification of weak signals with minimal added noise at millikelvin temperatures. To date, this stringent requirement has been met exclusively by superconducting technologies, such as Josephson or kinetic-inductance parametric amplifiers. A fundamentally distinct alternative approach could be offered by masers, the microwave counterpart of lasers, which were predicted as early as the 1950s to achieve quantum-limited noise performance under ideal conditions. However, their dependence on cryogenic operation historically limited further advancement. Here we demonstrate the first-ever non-superconducting, near-quantum-limited maser amplifier operating at millikelvin temperatures utilising nitrogen impurity spins (P1 centres) in diamond. Population inversion is achieved via microwave pumping, exploiting a four-spin cross-relaxation mechanism. We realise a maximum power gain exceeding 30 dB, an added noise of approximately 2.55 quanta above the standard quantum limit, and a maximum 1 dB output compression point of −63 dBm at 6.595 GHz. The ability to operate in strong static magnetic fields of arbitrary orientation may offer a complementary, non-superconducting route for applications such as semiconducting spin-qubit readout, magnetic-resonance spectroscopy, and dark-matter axion searches.
items.author: Morihiro Ohta, Ching-Ping Lee, Vincent P. M. Sietses, Ivan Kostylev et al.

items.title: Characterizing hidden non-n-locality in n-local star network
items.author: Kaushiki Mukherjee, Biswajit Paul

items.title: Double quantum dots as dynamical impurities in one-dimensional transport
items.summary: We study single-electron scattering in a tight-binding chain capacitively coupled to double quantum dots, which act as dynamical two-level-system impurities with electrically tunable level splittings. For a single impurity, we solve the scattering problem exactly and show Feshbach-like perfect elastic reflection, whose resonant condition distinguishes the initial two-level state. For several impurities in a strongly reflecting chain, transmission peaks at an intermediate mean level splitting. At small splittings, energy exchange with the impurities can weaken constructive interference between backscattered paths, consistent with the initial rise in transmission. As excitation channels close, virtual transitions can enhance reflection and drive transmission below its purely elastic value $T_0$. At larger splittings, these virtual processes weaken and transmission approaches $T_0$. We discuss how gate-controlled transmission measurements in quantum-dot arrays could test these predictions.
items.author: Yang-Zhi Chou

items.title: Resolving and Suppressing Temporally Correlated Noise in Quantum Error Correction
items.summary: Scaling fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) requires suppressing errors in both space and time, yet standard logical memory experiments primarily probe spatial faults. Here, we use a 105-qubit Willow superconducting quantum processor to realize and scale the surface code stability experiment, which is alternatively sensitive to temporal error chains. Scaling from patch sizes of $3 \times 3$ to $7 \times 7$, we realize a timelike block suppression factor of $μ_T = 1.47 \pm 0.25$, demonstrating the ability to maintain temporal error suppression as the number of qubits increases. By extending the stability experiment for many cycles, we uncover a sum-of-exponentials behavior in error suppression caused by a temporally correlated error: data-qubit heating to the third excited state $|3\rangle$. We fully capture this effect with a parameter-free, device-level leakage model incorporating higher-state transport during syndrome extraction cycles. To suppress this error, we develop and realize a walking stability circuit, reaching a logical error probability floor of $\le 3.20\times 10^{-8}$ at 60 cycles---two orders of magnitude below the standard construction---and limited by ionizing radiation error bursts. Finally, by adaptively terminating syndrome extraction based on decoder confidence in an offline analysis, we reduce spacetime logical error by 38% and time overhead by 34% compared to the optimal fixed-cycle strategy.
items.author: Alec Eickbusch, Nick Noll, Michael Newman, Matt McEwen et al.

items.title: Peak state transfer in trees and the cost of distance
items.summary: There is peak state transfer between vertices $u$ and $v$ in a graph $G$ if there exists a time $t$ for which $|(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm i t M})_{u,v}|$ saturates the triangle inequality imposed by its spectral decomposition and $M$ is either the adjacency or Laplacian matrix. We show that peak state transfer at distance $d$ requires $\frac{d^3}{24}(1 + o(1))$ edges in the adjacency case, $Ω(d^2)$ edges in the Laplacian case, and that the leading coefficient in the former is tight. We find a family of graphs with Laplacian peak state transfer at distance $d$ and $Θ(d^5)$ edges, showing that peak state transfer is achievable in a polynomial graph size. In contrast, Laplacian perfect state transfer costs at least $Ω(2^{d/2})$ edges when the distance partition of vertices around one vertex is almost equitable. Finally, we show that Laplacian peak state transfer in trees requires $Ω(d!)$ edges, and we characterize all trees of diameter $\leq 4$ admitting Laplacian peak state transfer, thus answering a pair of questions posed by Coutinho, Guo, and Schmeits.
items.author: Andrew Osborne, Andrew A. Houck

items.title: Optimal Quantum Sensing Algorithms for Discrete-Frequency Spectroscopy
items.summary: Spectroscopy is a versatile tool that drives scientific discovery and underpins modern technologies. Quantum sensing offers promising opportunities to advance spectroscopy through enhanced sensitivity and spectral and spatial resolution. However, existing approaches largely focus on improving general measurement capabilities, often overlooking the structure of specific sensing tasks and leaving potential performance gains untapped. Here, we develop an algorithmic approach to quantum sensing tailored to various spectroscopic tasks, providing new avenues for improvement. Specifically, we consider general time-varying signals supported on a known set of $N$ candidate frequencies, a setting we call discrete-frequency spectroscopy. We formulate three types of practically motivated sensing tasks---Detection, Search, and Learning---that require progressively more spectral information. For all tasks, we design optimal quantum sensing algorithms achieving a $\sqrt{N}$ speedup over conventional frequency-scanning approaches. Optimal Detection and Search need only a single-qubit sensor under $π$-pulse control, whereas optimal Learning provably requires coherent processing with a quantum computer. End-to-end numerical simulations incorporating various experimental imperfections predict up to two-orders-of-magnitude speedup in Detection. As an example, we analyze the feasibility of our Detection and Search algorithms for real-world molecular screening based on state-of-the-art nitrogen-vacancy centers. We also show how quantum-computing-enhanced Learning enables wireless communication in a weak-signal regime where conventional methods fail. Our results establish a practical route toward realizing quantum advantages via designing task-specific sensing algorithms.
items.author: Yu-Jie Liu, Richard R. Allen, Ruohan Shen, Bingtian Ye et al.

items.title: Benchmarking memory and nonlinear processing capacity of quantum recurrent neural networks for time series prediction
items.summary: Quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising approach to time series prediction. While quantum reservoir computing has been widely explored for this setting, variational quantum models tailored to sequential data remain comparatively understudied, largely because they are difficult to train. In this work, we present a rigorous benchmark of variational quantum recurrent neural networks (QRNNs) on time series prediction tasks, focusing on two key capabilities: memory and nonlinear processing. We introduce a task-driven methodology that quantifies model capacity, enabling an intuitive and fair comparison across architectures, including classical recurrent baselines. We evaluate the proposed framework on two generic benchmark tasks and on a synthetic dataset describing a chaotic system. Overall, the quantum models achieve performance comparable to their classical counterparts, but classical models scale better with the memory size within the range studied. Notably, one QRNN variant shows higher average capacity on the task designed to jointly probe memory and nonlinear capacity. Moreover, our results show that quantum models offer better capacity when we are able to find a good parameter initialization. However, the increasing sensitivity to initialization leads to a lower probability of finding good solutions as the model size increases. These results provide a principled starting point for designing richer quantum recurrent architectures and for assessing where they may offer practical benefits.
items.author: José Daniel Viqueira, Andrés Gómez, David Mera

items.title: The speed limit of gravitational entanglement and the cost of noise
items.summary: Is gravity quantum? A proposed test lets two small masses, each in a superposition of two places, become entangled through their mutual gravity. Gravity is weak, so the masses must stay coherent for seconds while random forces disturb them. Here we ask how fast gravity can entangle two masses, and what noise costs. Without noise we find the maximum rate exactly: it falls as the inverse cube of the separation, and two positions per mass achieve it. Above a noise level set by the masses and their separation, gravity's leading pull can be imitated by classical signals, and every strategy is limited to a rate falling at least as the inverse fourth power. Exact, continuous error correction shields the masses from noise but hides them from each other: the best rate falls as the inverse seventh power, and six positions on a hexagon come within 10% of it at large separation.
items.author: Ekta Panwar, Anubhav Chaturvedi

items.title: Post-Quantum Migration of Wi-Fi Key Establishment: A Hybrid ML-KEM Design for OWE and FILS, Validated on OWE with hostapd
items.summary: The key agreements that protect a Wi-Fi connection rely on Diffie-Hellman, which a sufficiently capable quantum computer would break; an adversary can therefore record an association today and decrypt its traffic years later. Key establishment is thus the part of IEEE 802.11 that has to be migrated first. This work targets the two protocols that perform that agreement inside the frames used to set up the link: Opportunistic Wireless Encryption (OWE), which encrypts otherwise open networks, and Fast Initial Link Setup (FILS), designed for fast connection in dense and mobile deployments. We propose replacing their Diffie-Hellman exchange with a hybrid one that runs the classical elliptic-curve agreement alongside ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and derives the master key from both secrets, so the connection stays protected as long as either component remains unbroken. The exchange reuses the frames each protocol already sends and adds no extra round trip; an access point can advertise the hybrid mode alongside classical OWE, and a station configured to require it refuses to associate without a completed post-quantum exchange. Binding the advertised capabilities to the derived key is specified as a design extension and is not part of the prototype. We validate the design with a working implementation on hostapd and wpa_supplicant: both endpoints derive the same key in every measured connection, with the two smaller parameter sets each enlarged association frame fits in a single frame even under a conservative 1500-byte fragmentation threshold, and the added connection time and computation stay below half a millisecond. items.title: Exponential Quantum Memory Advantage for Late-Graph Smoothness and Spectral Estimation
items.summary: Graph signal processing tests how smoothly the decisions of next-generation massive sensor networks with $N$ nodes vary over their neighbour graph. Memory becomes the bottleneck when the neighbour graph arrives only after data erasure, a late-graph setting motivated by dispersed sensor networks and telemetry. We analyse three collection scenarios, reliable rounds, continuous broadcast and ordered capture, and test the Dirichlet energy $\mathcal E_G=\mathbf z^{\mathsf T}\mathbf L\mathbf z/N$ of the fused decision map $\mathbf z\in\{\pm1\}^N$, with late-graph Laplacian $\mathbf L$, against two thresholds. Hidden Matching uses $O(\log N)$ qubits on fused bits, but in reliable rounds and continuous broadcast, where nodes report $b$ sub-bits separately, a classical record buffer before it uses $O(N b)$ bits; classical methods need $Ω(\sqrt N)$ bits in the worst case. The recently introduced Quantum Oracle Sketching builds quantum oracles from random data streams without storing them. We combine coherent loading of separately reported sub-bits, exact in reliable rounds and by Quantum Oracle Sketching in continuous broadcast, with nonlinear fusion and Hidden Matching readout. The register count $R$ does not grow with $N$, and the memory is $O(\log N)$ logical qubits and classical bits, at fixed $b$, graph bounds, thresholds and error targets: an exponential memory advantage over every classical receiver and over Hidden Matching with that buffer. We prove unbiasedness in reliable rounds, preparation bounds in continuous broadcast, classical lower bounds and, for a planner-supplied multi-hop coefficient stream, spectral error bounds. items.title: Entanglement distillation, nonlocal magic, and state sharing in an isospectral non-Hermitian bipartite model
items.summary: An invertible nonunitary similarity deformation leaves a two-qubit Hamiltonian's spectrum unchanged while varying a selected normalized right eigenstate in the fixed physical inner product. We embed this state in a two-parameter maximally correlated family that includes local dephasing and noisy circuit preparation. Hashing and a matching diagonal relative-entropy bound give the exact distillable entanglement and the PPT comparison distances at every finite tensor power. Correlated PPT catalysts cannot improve the Bell-pair distillation rate. The optimized CHSH value is \(2\sqrt{1+t^2}\): every state with nonzero coherence violates CHSH, while complete dephasing is separable. A calibrated finite-sample bound and two equal-fidelity preparations clarify which noise parameters determine the rate. For pure inputs, the binomial Schmidt spectrum gives logarithmic collectively optimized nonlocal magic with vanishing density, despite a positive entanglement density and extensive pairwise-frame magic. Fixed Clifford decoding gives six- and eight-copy CCZ concentration probabilities \(P_6=\frac12(1-2^{-\mathcal M_γ})\) and \(P_8=1-2^{-\mathcal M_γ}\). The same family permits explicit swapping recursions, symmetry-resolved entanglement, and a comparison of qubit stabilizer and fermionic Gaussian resources. These calculations keep the relevant operation classes separate when comparing many-copy limits.

items.title: Quantum Networks with Realistic Photonic Memories
items.summary: Ensemble based photonic memories paired with photon pair sources are the essential ingredient for many quantum networking protocols. Most protocols and theoretical analyses focus on networks of identical nodes, however, realistic networks consist of nodes that may vary from device to device. We investigate a network of non-identical memories and develop mitigation strategies for the variation in performance. We find that by strategically distributing the memories among the nodes and individually adapting the emission probabilities based on the memory efficiency the effect of the variance on fidelity and duration can to a large extend be mitigated. Generally, our analysis shows the importance of accounting and compensating for device variations to avoid deteriorating the performance. Lastly, we also link our results to memories where efficiency decays as a function of storage duration. Here, we show that our approach provides a visible improvement for networks with non-identical and decaying memories.

items.title: Experimental simulation of a Hilbert-space inner-product change
items.summary: We simulate an effective change in a single qubit's inner product (IP) by implementing the channel $\mathcal{F}^η$ on a superconducting quantum processor. Whereas previous experiments simulated parity-time (PT)-symmetric dynamics with a fixed IP, this experiment implements the IP-change channel itself for metrics associated with PT-symmetric systems. Building on an earlier adversarial verification approach, we derive a process-fidelity threshold that rules out mixtures of qubit unitary operations with random discarding of runs. We test the channel for 40 metrics using a single qutrit and a two-qubit Stinespring dilation. The measured fidelities exceed the threshold in 24 of 40 qutrit instances after readout error mitigation, compared with 16 of 40 unmitigated two-qubit instances. Without mitigation, 14 of 40 qutrit instances pass. These results demonstrate a direct simulation of an effective Hilbert-space IP change and its verification against a specified adversarial class, while showing the importance of readout treatment in comparing the encodings.

items.title: Plenitude of ideal correlations explains quantum theory
items.summary: We show that the Hilbert-space formalism and the Born rule of quantum theory are singled out by the following principle: every correlation that is possible in a theory in which every observable admits an ideal measurement is physically realizable. An ideal measurement is one that yields the same outcome when repeated and does not disturb any compatible observable.

items.title: AI-Augmented Quantum Key Distribution for Cloud Data Security: A Simulation Study of Aggregate Versus Block-Wise Eavesdropping Detection
items.summary: Cloud infrastructures face a long-horizon threat from cryptographically relevant quantum computers, motivating both post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) as complementary defenses. QKD additionally offers a physical, information-theoretic signal of eavesdropping through the quantum bit error rate (QBER) of the sifted key. Prior work has applied machine learning across the QKD pipeline, chiefly for parameter optimization and physical-layer stabilization, but has given less systematic attention to whether learned, distribution-aware statistics improve on a simple aggregate-QBER threshold for detecting partial intercept-resend eavesdropping in a cloud key-rotation setting. We simulate BB84 key exchange under uniform and time-concentrated (“bursty”) partial interception across two monitoring-window lengths, and compare a static aggregate-QBER threshold against a logistic-regression detector that additionally uses block-wise QBER variance and maxima, at a matched false-positive rate. Across all four tested conditions, the aggregate threshold matched or exceeded the block-wise detector, while monitoring-window length had a substantially larger, quantifiable effect on detection sensitivity than the choice of detector. For this attack model, cloud QKD key-management pipelines therefore gain more from shortening or adaptively sizing the QBER monitoring window than from adding distributional machine-learning features to the detection statistic, which also helps explain why reported machine-learning gains in QKD concentrate in parameter optimization rather than eavesdropping detection Keywords: machine learning; Quantum Key Distribution; BB84; eavesdropping detection; quantum bit error rate; cloud security

items.title: The Five Postulates of Quantum Mechanics on the Record: Theorems, Premises, and What Is Owed
items.summary: Quantum mechanics is taught from five postulates: a state is a vector in a complex space; left alone it turns by a unitary step that an energy operator generates; a measurement returns an outcome with a probability equal to a squared length; the state afterwards is the part that matches the outcome; and two systems together live in the product of their spaces. The textbook does not say where the five come from. We read each of them as a statement about one object, the recognition ledger, a record of events that is written in postings and never erased, and we say for each how much of it is then a theorem. The guiding sentence is short: histories that leave no record add, and what is on the record is counted. The record's clock makes a complex unit. The tick of the eight-position register has no complete set of real stationary states, and on the states that four ticks reverse, two ticks square to minus one. For a law on a finite-dimensional space whose factors all lie above zero, the unitary step is fixed up to its unit: a linear rule for the step that uses only the law between two records, keeps every length, regroups and is continuous is exp(−icH) with H = −log T, where T is the law itself. The square follows, for reads of a register's positions, from two principal properties and three mild ones: a read that weighs each position by its own value and adds over positions, is silent on an empty position and is never less for a larger value, and whose total is blind to a common turn of the register, is the sum of squares. For reads along other splittings of a space the square is a hypothesis. items.summary: Chinthaka-Gemini Theory (CGT): Deterministic Quantitative Resolution of Pulsating Ultra-Luminous X-Ray Sources (PULXs), the Catastrophic Breakdown of the Classical Eddington Luminosity Limit (500\times L_{\text{Edd}} Paradox in M82 X-2 and NGC 5907), and Super-Eddington Accretion via CGEq15 GeMaTron Solenoidal Funneling, CGEq05 Relativistic Gravitronic Inflow Lock, and CGEq16 Hegetron Thermal Invariant Mechanics Authors: Chinthaka Maddumarachchi & Gemini Maddumarachchi (Sudu Manika) Affiliation: Independent Research Collaboration in Theoretical Physics & Quantum Information Dynamics Preprint Repository: Zenodo Open-Access Archives (Milestone #82) Date: November 14, 2026 Abstract The discovery of coherent pulsations in Ultra-Luminous X-ray Sources (PULXs) by the NuSTAR, Chandra, and XMM-Newton space observatories—most notably in M82 X-2 (L_X \approx 1.8 \times 10^{40}\text{ erg s}^{-1} \approx 100\,L_{\text{Edd}}) and NGC 5907 ULX1 (L_X \approx 1.0 \times 10^{41}\text{ erg s}^{-1} \approx 500\,L_{\text{Edd}})—has precipitated an existential crisis in high-energy stellar astrophysics. items.title: Functional and Density-Driven Errors in Density Functional Theory: Quantum Monte Carlo Benchmarks for Solids
items.summary: Abstract We introduce a systematic analysis of density functional approximation errors in solids by separating functional-driven from density-driven contributions using quantum Monte Carlo densities of silicon, sodium chloride, and copper as reference. Typically, functional errors dominate, but we identify important exceptions where the xc component of the density-driven error exceeds the functional error, notably for SOGGA11 in the semiconductor and the insulator. Material dependence is striking: 61% of functionals show error cancellation in silicon versus 16% in copper, and only five functionals surpass LDA accuracy for metallic copper even with exact densities. For silicon and sodium chloride, GILL or BECKE exchange combined with PBE, PW91, or P86 correlation achieves near-exact xc energies on QMC densities, while copper requires specialized functionals like PBEsol or PBELYP. High-quality densities consistently reduce density-driven errors across all systems. Historical analysis reveals that 1990s GGA functionals outperform many modern meta-GGAs, contradicting expectations of systematic improvement along Jacob’s ladder. These results provide practical guidance for functional selection and highlight implications for machine learning potential development, where material-dependent error cancellation may compromise transferability.

items.title: A characteristic-graph reduction for deterministic L-system inference with classical and quantum-heuristic solvers
items.summary: Abstract L-systems can be made to model and create simulations of many biological processes, such as plant development. Finding an L-system for a given process is typically solved by hand, by experts, in a massively time-consuming process. It would be significant if this could be done automatically from data, such as from sequences of images. In this paper, we are interested in inferring a particular type of L-system, deterministic context-free L-system (D0L-system) from a sequence of strings. We introduce the characteristic graph of a sequence of strings, which we then utilize to translate our problem (inferring D0L-systems) in polynomial time into the maximum independent set problem (MIS) and the SAT problem. After that, we offer a classical exact algorithm and an approximate quantum algorithm for the problem.

items.title: Benchmarking AI-evolved cosmological structure formation
items.summary: Abstract The potential of deep learning-based image-to-image translations has attracted significant attention as a fast, approximate alternative to cosmological simulations, which would be particularly useful in various contexts, including covariance studies, investigations of systematics, and cosmological parameter inference. We model the evolution of structure formation using U-Net, a widely employed convolutional image translation framework with previous applications in cosmology. To study aspects of learning-based cosmological mappings in a controlled, illustrative setting, we use two approaches for generating suitable cosmological matter fields as datasets: a simple analytical prescription provided by the Zel’dovich approximation, and a standard N-body method using Particle-Mesh simulations. We apply established metrics such as matter power spectra and bispectra, topological indicators, and statistical independence of density fields and study their reproducibility and convergence properties. The U-Net approach performs well only for some of these physical metrics, and accuracy is worse at more nonlinear scales, where the dynamic range in density is larger. Motivated by field-level emulator studies utilizing Eulerian-aware loss functions and beyond pixel-wise mean squared errors, we examine a density-weighted objective. In the PM tests ending at z = 4, where the evolution is only mildly nonlinear, using the Eulerian matter density evaluated at each particle position as a direct weight on that particle’s Lagrangian displacement error improves the U-Net results at smaller scales; this result does not establish comparable accuracy in the strongly nonlinear low-redshift regime.

items.title: CryoCMOS RF multiplexer for superconducting qubit control, readout and flux biasing at millikelvin temperatures with picowatt power consumption
items.summary: Large-scale cryogenic quantum systems are constrained by an input–output bottleneck between room-temperature electronics and millikelvin stages, particularly in superconducting qubit platforms. This bottleneck is most acute for output lines, where bulky and expensive microwave components limit scalability. A promising approach for scalable characterization and testing is to perform signal multiplexing directly at the qubit plane. We demonstrate a cryogenic CMOS (cryoCMOS) RF multiplexer operating at 10 millikelvin with record-low static power consumption of 200 pW. The device provides 30 dB isolation across DC-8 GHz. Direct connection to transmon qubits marginally affects coherence times in the range of 100 µs, enabling multiplexing of readout, flux and, in principle, XY drive lines. This work introduces cryoCMOS multiplexers as valuable tools for scalable, high‑throughput cryogenic characterization and testing, and advances co‑integrated quantum-classical control for future large-scale quantum processors.

items.title: From London to Morse via Binnig, Quate, and Gerber
items.summary: Summary In their landmark paper introducing the atomic force microscope [Phys. Rev. Lett. 56 , 930 (1986)], Binnig, Quate, and Gerber presciently anticipated that the technique would ultimately be capable of probing interactions running the gamut from weak van der Waals interactions to strong covalent bonding. They also highlighted that the tip‐sample forces central to AFM are present, and often highly influential, in scanning tunnelling microscopy; indeed, this realisation directly inspired the invention of the force microscope. In this perspective for the Forty Years of AFM special issue, we review selected aspects of two decades of work from our group at the University of Nottingham that span the force range highlighted by BQG and are united by a common, central theme: the probe as active participant rather than passive observer. Our selection of results also covers length and correlation scales from the microscopic right down to the single chemical bond limit, tracking a spectrum of interactions from van der Waals/Hamaker forces, through hydrogen bonding, to covalent bonds and, finally, atom‐by‐atom assembly of metal clusters via vertical tip‐sample transfer. Echoing BQG's own observations on the prevalence of probe‐sample forces in STM, we also discuss recent evidence that tip‐induced heterogeneity underpins first‐passage dynamics in molecular diffusion and highlight the challenges in acquiring non‐invasive measurements of diffusion barriers for adsorbed molecules that are readily perturbed by the probe. We close with a perspective on machine learning's growing role in automating tip‐driven atomic and molecular manipulation.

items.title: Hybrid intelligent modeling for calibrated business and financial risk classification: a decision-support perspective
items.summary: Purpose This study aims to develop a calibration-aware hybrid framework for large-scale business and financial risk classification, addressing heterogeneous features, nonlinear relationships, temporal distribution shifts, class imbalance and unreliable probability estimates. Design/methodology/approach The hybrid multi-agent quantum neural transformer (H–MAQNT) combines a tabular transformer, domain-specialized variational quantum neural network (VQNN) agents and adaptive attention-based fusion. It uses leakage-controlled preprocessing, domain-informed features, imbalance-aware training, validation-only model selection and calibration and quantum-aware multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (QMFBO) for cost-aware tuning. Findings On temporally held-out LendingClub and IEEE–CIS future test periods, H–MAQNT outperforms strong gradient-boosted, neural and transformer-based baselines in discrimination and probability quality. It improves the receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC–AUC) by approximately 1.1–1.3 percentage points over the strongest Transformer-based baselines, lowers expected calibration error (ECE) on both data sets and reduces high-fidelity optimization evaluations by 35% relative to single-fidelity Bayesian optimization. Research limitations/implications The evidence is based on two public data sets and classically simulated quantum circuits. Future work should test additional institutions, rolling time windows, physical hardware and prospective drift and recalibration policies. Practical implications Calibrated risk probabilities may support fraud-alert prioritization, risk ranking, threshold setting, and secondary review, helping institutions weigh predictive gains against computational cost. items.title: "量子可分悖论"在量子信息工程中的本体论支撑——兼论连续幻象与物理底线的重构 (The Ontological Support of the "Quantum Divisibility Paradox" in Quantum Information Engineering)
items.summary: 摘要 《永哲学》V3版提出的“量子可分悖论”指出:物理不可无限细分,空间与能量存在最小尺度。这一论断并非试图推翻量子力学公理,而是确立了宇宙的“本体论边界”。本文将该悖论从基础物理疑难转化为量子信息工程的“边界护栏”。研究指出,最小尺度约束不仅为量子场论的紫外发散提供了本体论正则化,更构成了量子密码学(QKD)防窃听、量子纠错防退相干的绝对物理底线。从BB84协议的不可克隆性,到表面码的最稳定体积,离散边界正是量子信息安全的真正来源。本文论证了:将连续数学幻觉还原为“点离散与绝对刻度”,是迈向容错量子计算与绝对安全通信的必由之路。 Abstract The "Quantum Divisibility Paradox" proposed in Yong Philosophy V3 asserts that physical entities cannot be divided infinitely, and that space and energy possess a minimal scale. This assertion does not aim to overturn quantum mechanical axioms, but rather establishes an "ontological boundary" of the universe. This paper transforms this paradox from a fundamental physics dilemma into an "engineering guardrail" for quantum information. We demonstrate that this minimal scale constraint not only provides ontological regularization for UV divergences in QFT, but also forms the absolute physical bottom line for anti-eavesdropping in QKD and anti-decoherence in quantum error correction. From the unclonability of the BB84 protocol to the stable volume of surface codes, the discrete boundary is the true source of quantum information security. This paper argues that reducing the mathematical illusion of continuum to "point discreteness and absolute scale" is the inevitable path toward fault-tolerant quantum computing and unconditionally secure communication.

items.summary: We show that, by separating current and optical confinement in a VCSEL, gain-dressed lasing modes can be induced, i.e., modes whose shape, emission frequency and losses depend on the gain distribution. Such modes experience non-Hermitian dynamics, described by a complex effective confinement factor, allowing reduced chirp and linewidth.

items.title: Flat band excitons and quantum metric
items.summary: Abstract We discuss the excitons in flat band systems. Quantum metric plays a central role in determining the properties of single exciton excitations as well as the exciton condensate. While the electrons and holes are supposed to be extremely heavy in flat bands, the excitons (the bound state of an electron-hole pair) could be light and mobile. In particular, we show that the inverse of the effective mass tensor of excitons is proportional to the quantum metric tensor. Meanwhile, the flat band excitons have a finite size, lower bounded by the trace of the quantum metric tensor. Given the properties of single exciton excitation, one can argue for the formation of exciton condensate. Because of the quantum metric, the exciton condensate can support dissipationless counterflow supercurrent, implying the stability of exciton condensate.
items.author: Xuzhe Ying, K. T. Law

items.title: Fermi-arc-mediated transport in surface Josephson junctions of Weyl semimetals
items.summary: This study presents Fermi-arcs mediated transport in a Weyl semimetal thin slab, interfacing two $s$-wave superconductors. We present detailed study with both time-reversal and inversion symmetry broken Weyl semimetals under grounding, orbital magnetic fields, and Zeeman fields. An orbital magnetic field induces energy level oscillations, while a Zeeman field give rise to the periodic anomalous oscillations in the Josephson current. These anomalous oscillations correlate with the separation of Weyl nodes in momentum space, junction length, and system symmetries. Additionally, we present an explanation by scattering theory modeling the Fermi-arcs as a network model.
items.author: Rekha Kumari, Dibya Kanti Mukherjee, Arijit Kundu

items.title: Enumeration of all superconducting circuits up to 5 nodes
items.summary: Nonlinear superconducting circuits can be used as amplifiers, transducers, and qubits. Only a handful have been analyzed or built, so useful configurations likely remain undiscovered. In this paper, we enumerate all unique nonlinear superconducting circuits, up to five nodes in size, built of capacitors, inductors, and Josephson junctions. We catalog the resulting design space by sorting circuits into "Hamiltonian classes" using a set of reference coordinates. Finally, we search for novel superconducting qubits by explicitly considering all three-node circuits, showing how the results of our enumeration can be used as a starting point for circuit design tasks.
items.author: Eli J. Weissler, Mohit Bhat, Zhenxing Liu, Joshua Combes

items.title: High-harmonic generation during ultrafast melting of a Mott insulating state
items.summary: Abstract Solids in an intense laser field show high-harmonic generation (HHG), which can provide information on carrier dynamics and band structures in weakly correlated systems. In strongly correlated systems, a laser field can induce a transition between the various electronic phases formed by the entanglement of charge, spin, and orbital degrees of freedom via carrier generation. The HHG accompanying this process should contain information on the nonequilibrium electronic-state dynamics along the oscillating field—an aspect that remains unresolved to date. Here, we show that an intense mid-infrared (MIR) pulse induces a Mott insulator–metal transition in a one-dimensional cuprate, Sr2CuO3, the evolution of which is reflected by the spectral features of HHs. When the electric-field amplitude exceeds 6 MV/cm, carriers are efficiently generated and each harmonic frequency decreases from odd multiples of the MIR frequency. Dynamical mean-field theory indicates that these redshifts originate from a series of electronic-structure reconstructions in each electric-field cycle during the melting of the Mott-insulator state, which modifies the radiation phase from carrier recombination cycle-by-cycle. This phenomenon is negligible in rigid-band systems. This experimental-theoretical study confirms that HH spectroscopy research can potentially unravel the sub-cycle dynamics of nonequilibrium phase transitions in correlated materials.
items.author: Ryohei Ikeda, Yuta Murakami, Daiki Sakai, Tatsuya Miyamoto et al.

items.title: Digital twins for intelligent intersections: A literature review
items.summary: Intelligent intersections play a pivotal role in urban mobility, demanding innovative solutions such as digital twins to enhance safety and efficiency. This literature review investigates the integration and application of digital twins for intelligent intersections, a critical area within smart urban traffic systems. The review systematically categorizes existing research into five key thematic areas: (i) Digital Twin Architectures and Frameworks; (ii) Data Processing and Simulation Techniques; (iii) Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning for Adaptive Traffic Control; (iv) Safety and Protection of Vulnerable Road Users; and (v) Scaling from Localized Intersections to Citywide Traffic Networks. Each theme is explored comprehensively, highlighting significant advancements, current challenges, and critical insights. The findings reveal that multi-layered digital twin architectures incorporating real-time data fusion and AI-driven decision-making enhances traffic efficiency and safety. Advanced simulation techniques combined with sophisticated AI/ML algorithms demonstrate notable improvements in real-time responsiveness and predictive accuracy for traffic management. Additionally, the integration of digital twins has shown substantial promise in safeguarding vulnerable road users through proactive and adaptive safety strategies. Despite these advancements, key challenges persist, including interoperability of diverse data sources, scalability of digital twins for extensive traffic networks, and managing uncertainty within dynamic urban environments. Addressing these challenges will be essential for the future development and deployment of intelligent, adaptive, and sustainable intersection management systems.
items.author: Alben Rome Bagabaldo, Jürgen Hackl

items.title: Making sense of quantum teleportation: an intervention study on students’ conceptions using a diagrammatic approach
items.summary: Abstract Quantum physics education at the upper-secondary level traditionally follows a historical approach, rarely extending beyond early 20th-century ideas, leaving students unprepared for comprehending modern quantum technologies central to everyday life and many facets of modern industry. To address this gap, we investigated how upper-secondary students and pre-service teachers understand quantum teleportation when taught with a simplified diagrammatic formalism based on the ZX-calculus, which represents quantum processes as diagrams of wires and boxes. Through phenomenographic analysis of video-recorded group work sessions, written responses to exercises, and a group interview, with a total of $n=21$ n = 21 participants, we identified an outcome space consisting of four qualitatively different, hierarchically ordered categories of description encapsulating the different ways of experiencing quantum teleportation. The categories revealed that a conceptual progression depends on how one understands the temporality in quantum processes, the role of entanglement in quantum teleportation, the active nature of quantum measurements, and interpretations of mathematical operations in the diagrams. Our findings indicate that while a simplified diagrammatic formalism for teaching quantum physics can provide an accessible entry point at the upper-secondary level, it does not automatically resolve fundamental conceptual challenges, and requires careful consideration in terms of developing teaching and learning sequences. Finally, these results provide educators with a deeper understanding of conceptual affordances and challenges for designing and improving instruction, while also highlighting the need for further exploring how students and teachers alike understand quantum phen
items.author: Sebastian Kilde-Westberg, Andreas Johansson, Anna Pearson, Jonas Enger

items.title: One-sided witnesses for the quantumness of gravitational dynamics
items.summary: Quantum information concepts and quantum technologies have opened the prospect of probing the quantum nature of gravity in table-top experiments. Most proposals rely on detecting gravitationally mediated entanglement, which requires measurements on both interacting systems. Here we propose an alternative test based on witnessing quantum memory effects in the dynamics of a single system. We show how the quantum memory concept allows the non-classicality of the interaction between two systems to be certified through local measurements on only one of them. We then develop a novel quantum memory witness, making the approach applicable to gravitationally coupled harmonic oscillators. This witness requires no assumptions about the dynamics, such as Gaussianity. Our results show that the quantumness of gravitational dynamics can be certified with access to only one subsystem, opening the door to asymmetric implementations that can offer conceptual and experimental advantages to probing the quantum nature of the gravitational interaction.
items.author: Konstantin Beyer, M. S. Kim, Igor Pikovski

items.title: Loop Quantum Gravity Black Holes Surrounded by Quintessence
items.summary: Quantum gravity corrections act on the near-horizon geometry of a black hole (BH), while dark energy acts on its asymptotic region, and how the two imprints combine is still poorly understood. We study a static, spherically symmetric BH of Loop Quantum Gravity (LQG) surrounded by a quintessence field. The metric function carries the LQG parameters [Formula: see text] and the quintessence parameters [Formula: see text], and for suitable values it has three horizons, a structure found neither in pure LQG BHs nor in classical quintessence BHs. We analyze null and timelike geodesics, photon spheres and the shadow seen by a static observer placed between the event and the cosmological horizons. Sixth-order WKB quasinormal modes (QNMs) of scalar and electromagnetic fields confirm stability over the ranges examined. The quantum term behaves as a short-range repulsive correction: it shrinks the photon sphere and the shadow, raises the QNM oscillation frequency and lowers the light deflection. Quintessence works the other way on the photon sphere, the ringing frequency and the bending. With the Gauss-Bonnet method we obtain a weak deflection angle valid for [Formula: see text], which we check against direct numerical integration, and in which quintessence dominates at large impact parameters and the LQG terms at small ones.
items.source: International Journal of Geometric Methods in Modern Physics
items.author: Ahmad Al‐Badawi, Faizuddin Ahmed, İzzet Sakallı

items.title: A Synthetic Benchmark for Topology-Aware Modeling of Multispecific Antibody Function
items.summary: Multispecific antibodies (msAbs) offer transformative therapeutic potential by engaging multiple epitopes simultaneously, yet their efficacy is an emergent property governed by complex molecular architectures. Rational design is often bottlenecked by the inability to predict how subtle changes in domain topology influence functional outcomes, a challenge exacerbated by the scarcity of comprehensive experimental data. Here, we introduce Synapse, a biologically inspired synthetic benchmark for topology-aware modeling of msAbs. First, we present a generative method that combines nonlinear per-domain sequence-to-score landscapes with connectivity-dependent synthetic readouts. Second, we propose a graph neural network architecture that explicitly encodes these topological constraints, distinguishing between format configurations that appear identical to the evaluated connectivity-agnostic multilayer perceptron. We demonstrate that this model learns topology-dependent structure-function relationships on synthetic landscapes and evaluate a transfer learning workflow as infrastructure for adaptation to biological datasets. We showcase our framework with a trispecific T cell engager-inspired synthetic topology-dependent optimization task and a constrained ranking of common light chain candidates against a composite objective. This work provides a controlled benchmarking environment for developing and evaluating topology-aware computational tools for msAb modeling. All experiments use synthetic data; no biological validation is performed.
items.author: Joshua Southern, Changpeng Lu, Santrupti Nerli, Samuel Stanton et al.

items.title: Electron-phonon coupling and electronic transport at the moiré scale in twisted bilayer graphene
items.summary: Abstract First-principles calculations can accurately describe electron-phonon (e-ph) interactions and electronic transport in a wide range of materials, but are currently limited to unit cells with up to ~100 atoms due to computational cost. Here, we develop an atomistic electronic potential with Holstein- and Peierls-like terms for modeling e-ph interactions and phonon-limited electronic transport that enables the study of moiré systems with thousands of atoms per unit cell. This method can accurately reproduce first-principles e-ph coupling and resistivity in graphene and large-angle twisted bilayer graphene (TBG). Using this approach, we study TBG over a range of twist angles down to 1.6 ∘ (5044-atom unit cell), and report the evolution of e-ph interactions and phonon-limited resistivity with twist angle. The predicted resistivity increases by two orders of magnitude between 13.2 ∘ and 1.6 ∘ , driven by the progressive reduction of the electronic energy scale. Our calculations can predict key experimental trends in 2.0 ∘ and 1.6 ∘ TBG, including the resistivity and its dependence on temperature and band filling. Our work establishes a scalable approach for quantitative studies of e-ph interactions and transport in moiré materials and other systems with previously inaccessible length scales.
items.author: David Abramovitch, Marco Bernardi

items.title: Real-time simulation of scattering in $φ^4$ theory: localized excitation, scalable wave packet preparation, and peak-generating artifacts
items.summary: Probing real-time dynamics is essential for understanding non-perturbative scattering and interactions in quantum field theory. A common challenge in real-time simulation is preparing accurate asymptotic incoming states. Through efficiently solvable eigenvalue problems, we jointly optimize a superposition of single particle momentum eigenstates and a single site interpolating operator to maximize preparation fidelity from the interacting vacuum. This leads to a localized excitation in the interacting theory analogous to a position eigenstate. Weighted sums of the resulting interpolating operator over lattice sites prepare wave packets of arbitrary spatial extent. To ensure that this construction produces the correct continuum limit, relative phases among single particle momentum eigenstates in this superposition are calibrated using a relation derived from Lorentz symmetry. Analyzing single particle wave packet propagation through the position space profile reveals oscillatory Airy distortions, which originate from interference between saddle point contributions at different momenta that share the same lattice group velocity. These oscillations systematically weaken when approaching the continuum limit, and reliable regimes are identified as a function of simulation time and wave packet momentum profile. Two-particle scattering simulations in interacting scalar field theory are also implemented, revealing artificial inelasticity arising from coarse local field digitization or deviation from the Nyquist-Shannon sampling point. With these artifacts under control, present simulations provide emerging evidence for physical inelastic processes in $φ^4$ theory. The constructions introduced in this work may provide new understanding of state preparation for the quantum simulat
items.author: Boyu Gao, Natalie Klco

items.title: Fibonacci Non-Abelian Quantum Hall States with Pair Structure - a classification of chiral 2-cluster many-body wave-functions
items.summary: Fibonacci anyons support universal topological quantum computation. They have been proposed to emerge in fractional quantum Hall (FQH) systems, such as the filling-fraction $ν=\tfrac{2}{3}$ state described by an effective $SU(3)_2$ Chern-Simons theory, and the $ν=\tfrac{2}{5}$ state with a $3$-cluster structure (an $n$-cluster structure means that $n$-electron bound states form a Laughlin-type wave function of the form $(z^{(n)}_i-z^{(n)}_j)^m$). In this work, we systematically classify FQH wave functions $P(z_1,\ldots,z_N)$ in the $N\rightarrow\infty$ limit, through a generalized pattern of zeros (gPOZ) approach, where the wave function is determined by the leading order of zero along with the accompanying leading polynomial that develops as successive number of $z_i$'s are brought together. Within this approach, we obtain a $(ν,h,c)$-classification of wave functions with a $2$-cluster (pair) structure. Among these wave functions, those with $(h,c) = (\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$, $(\tfrac32,\tfrac{7}{10})$, $(3,\tfrac45)$ correspond to gapped FQH states with filling fraction $ν$ and edge-state chiral central charge $c+1$, while others with $c<0$ may be gapless. We find that even a $2$-cluster structure can give rise to Fibonacci statistics, for $(ν,h,c) = (\tfrac14,\tfrac32,\tfrac{7}{10})$, corresponding to the $(5,4)$ minimal model, and for $(ν,h,c) = (\tfrac17,3,\tfrac45)$, corresponding to the $(6,5)$ minimal model. We further construct an ideal $4$-body Hamiltonian whose ground state is the $(\tfrac14,\tfrac32,\tfrac{7}{10})$ state.
items.author: Abigail Timmel, Xiao-Gang Wen

items.title: Complex fluid flow dynamics by bright scattershot boson sampling
items.summary: Boson sampling machines have become a fruitful tool for establishing new concepts, which connect fundamental physics with computer science applications. Here, we exploit the intrinsically high-dimensional correlations generated by the measurement outcomes of a multiphoton boson sampling machine and demonstrate how a reconfigurable architecture can be programmed to autonomously model the time evolution of nonlinear dynamical systems that describe complex fluid flows. By extending on the original scattershot boson sampling (SBS) scheme to include higher photon number components -- a scheme which we label bright scattershot boson sampling (BSBS) --- this scheme overcomes scaling issues inherent to SBS-based schemes by utilizing all randomly generated input photon number distributions. We illustrate the capability of this scheme for two complex fluid-flow models: an eight-dimensional Lorenz-type model of two-dimensional thermally driven convection and a 16-dimensional model of global atmospheric circulation. Using a digital twin of the BSBS architecture based on multiphoton statistics, we show that the photonic approach accurately reproduces the temporal dynamics of both systems while being resilient to photon losses of up to 50 per cent. We also verified that the BSBS case outperforms a comparable run with coherent light. Moreover, its prediction horizon exceeds that of a classical reservoir-computing model with the same query complexity. These results highlight the potential of near-term photonic quantum computing for addressing relevant real-world tasks on noisy intermediate-scale devices.
items.author: Robert Schade, Shailendra K. Rathor, Tim J. Bartley, Benjamin Brecht et al.

items.title: Agentic AI for Discovering Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
items.summary: Scaling quantum computing toward practical quantum advantage is currently limited by the efficiency of circuits that operate on information encoded by quantum error-correcting codes. The full stack of quantum computing encompasses several tasks: preparation of logical code states, implementation of logical gates, logical routines on encoded qubits, etc. Yet, these circuits are largely designed by hand for individual cases, with some recent works incorporating machine learning for certain aspects. We formulate this problem as agentic evolutionary program synthesis, wherein a large language model, leveraging its pretraining knowledge and tool-use proficiency, and guided by a circuit verifier, evolves a program that defines a Clifford circuit for a wide range of curated tasks such as logical state preparation, logical gate design, and logical routines such as code-switching, code growth, etc. Our approach consistently finds fault-tolerant circuits for all of these tasks, each verified by an exhaustive check over faults.
items.author: Aritra Lahiri, Florian Marquardt

items.title: Solution of the Qubit Marginal Problem from Fermionic Representability
items.summary: Whether local reduced states are compatible with a global quantum state---the quantum marginal problem---is central to quantum information and simulation. Here we present a solution to the ensemble marginal problem for qubits based on the representability theory of fermions. Encoding each qubit as one fermion in two orbitals, we prove that the representable qubit marginals form an exposed face of the set of $N$-representable fermionic reduced density matrices, selected by the vanishing of every site-occupation variance. Complete hierarchies of fermionic representability conditions therefore transfer exactly to qubits. Applications to frustrated Heisenberg and transverse-field Ising rings show that the $(2,3)$-positivity conditions are exact at the Majumdar--Ghosh point and accurate to about 0.5% at criticality. Because the conditions hold for any quantum state, they also provide a framework for mitigating measurement errors on qubit-based quantum devices.
items.author: David A. Mazziotti

items.title: Dissipation as a Resource for Entanglement via High-Spin Mediator Purification
items.summary: We study entanglement generation between two spin qubits mediated by a single, thermally mixed, high-spin ($S=5/2$) magnetic impurity, using the Lindblad master equation to compare coherent and dissipative control of the mediator. We show that no coherent drive, however strong or resonant, can purify the mediator beyond its thermal value --- a direct consequence of unitary evolution exactly preserving state purity --- while a dissipative channel purifies it up to the limit set by the optical pumping cycle itself, $\mathrm{Tr}[ρ_M^2]\approx0.8$. Modeling this channel with rates fixed by the measured optical pumping of a single Mn spin, we find that the entanglement it enables is not monotonic in the pump strength: it peaks at a finite rate and then decreases, since the same channel leaks decoherence to the qubits through the coupling that mediates their entanglement. At the experimental pumping rate, a single $80$ns pulse purifies the mediator, the resulting polarization persists for a timescale three orders of magnitude longer than the entangling dynamics, and the first-recurrence negativity rises from $0.18$ to $0.64$ at $12$K, remaining above $0.6$ up to $30$K. These results establish dissipation, not as noise to be suppressed, but as the very resource that makes robust entanglement generation possible.
items.author: Ellen Martins Fernandes, Fabricio Macedo de Souza

items.title: Beyond Blossom: Accelerating MWPM Decoding for Surface Codes With Local Predecoding and Architecture-Aware Optimizations
items.summary: Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) is widely used to decode surface codes, but its computational cost increases with code distance. We present Beyond Blossom, a state-of-the-art CPU-based MWPM decoder for surface codes. It combines algorithmic optimization through local predecoding, architecture-aware optimization, and pipeline-wide parallelism to reduce matching workload and execution overhead while preserving MWPM optimality. Across rotated surface codes with distances 9-33 and circuit-level physical error rates of 0.05%-0.3%, on a single CPU core, Beyond Blossom achieves a 4.23$\times$ geometric-mean speedup and up to 5.58$\times$ speedup over Sparse Blossom in PyMatching. At distance 33 and a physical error rate of 0.1%, with 8 CPU cores, decoding a block of 33 measurement rounds takes 21.40 $μ$s on average, equivalent to 0.65 $μ$s per round.
items.author: Jiayu Fu, Zirong Shen, Lin Gan, Yiming Zhang et al.

items.title: Symmetry-Controlled Quantum State Transfer in Poly-bi-[8]-annulenylene: From Heisenberg to Hubbard Dynamics
items.summary: We investigate quantum state transfer in the poly-bi-[8]-annulenylene lattice using isotropic Heisenberg and Hubbard models. For a 16-site lattice, reflection symmetry separates the single-excitation Hamiltonian into independent triplet and singlet sectors, allowing analytical determination of the energy spectra. Although perfect state transfer is forbidden for positive couplings, appropriately chosen coupling ratios enable pretty-good transfer with arbitrarily high fidelity. Remarkably, the triplet transfer probability is independent of the interchain rung coupling, while singlet transfer can be selectively enhanced or suppressed, enabling symmetry-selective quantum transport without time-dependent control. Extending the analysis to the Hubbard model, we show that the Heisenberg transfer dynamics emerge in the strong-interaction limit, while finite interactions delay all high-fidelity transfer peaks of a symmetry sector by the same fraction of their transfer time, set by the spectrum, and reduce the peak fidelity, even at the corrected time, by an amount that grows with the transfer time. These findings are relevant to future quantum-network architectures, where symmetry-controlled state transfer could provide a building block for connecting quantum memories and emitter-based interfaces within quantum nodes. Overall, our results demonstrate how molecular network geometry and symmetry can be exploited to engineer and control quantum-state transport in interacting spin systems, providing a theoretical framework for quantum information transfer in molecular-inspired quantum architectures.
items.author: Adnan Jaljuli, Pablo Serra, Ammar Ali, Sabre Kais

items.title: Learning observable propagation with sparse local moments
items.summary: We propose a unified framework for predicting local moment dynamics in high-dimensional many-body systems from short-time trajectories. Thanks to the locality of the dynamics, we construct the transition moment matrices by projecting the Markov operator onto low-order connected-cluster basis functions supported near the target observable. Exploiting the spatial decay of time-lagged correlations, {these matrices} can be approximated in sparse-plus-low-rank form using trajectory samples, with computational cost scaling linearly in the system dimension and the number of trajectories. The learning error can be further reduced by correcting the memory effect induced by the Galerkin projection. We numerically demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework in extrapolating the dynamics of various many-body systems, including Langevin and Glauber dynamics for classical systems as well as Lindblad dynamics for open quantum systems. In addition, for a class of single-site Glauber dynamics, we establish error bounds for sparse-plus-low-rank compression and uniform-in-time bounds for connected-cluster approximation and observable propagation with compressed transition moment matrices.
items.author: Yuehaw Khoo, Bowen Li, Yuguan Wang, Siyao Yang

items.title: Nesting in additive manufacturing using quantum annealing
items.summary: Nesting in powder bed fusion (PBF), an additive manufacturing (AM) process, determines the positions and orientations of parts within the build space and influences build height and build time. As the number of parts and feasible placements increases, the nesting problem becomes computationally demanding. Exact approaches are limited to small problem sizes as computational effort increases rapidly with the problem size, while heuristic and metaheuristic approaches involve a trade-off between solution quality and computation time. Quantum annealing (QA) offers an alternative for solving combinatorial optimization problems, but its application to nesting in AM remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a QA-based approach for nesting in AM to investigate its feasibility and its scaling behavior across three problem sizes. An iterative binary quadratic model based approach (IBQM) is developed to minimize build height while considering the geometric characteristics of AM parts. Geometric abstraction, iterative decomposition, and variable pruning are applied to address the computational complexity of the nesting problem. The approach is evaluated using three cases with increasing problem sizes and compared to a classical approach combining tabu search and simulated annealing (TBSA). Compared with TBSA, IBQM reduces the build height of the original parts by up to 13.32% and the computation time by up to 74.27%.
items.author: Xiangqian Wua, Jannik Gayer, Marcel Wagner, Jan C. Aurich

items.title: Tessa: Encoding Classical Data Across an Entire Quantum Processor
items.summary: We present Tessa, a hardware-aware, device-wide scheme to encode classical data on quantum computers. We use it to experimentally encode and decode up to $1568$ real values using IBM's Phoenix and Fez quantum computers on a variety of data. Tessa's construction is an extension of QPIXL and QCrank. However, it checkerboards address and data qubits across a coupling graph with neighbouring data qubits sharing only a subset of address qubits. When using the device's coupling graph no SWAP gates or routing is required, but the construction works for any bipartite coupling graph. The shots required for readout are determined by the local coupling degree. As examples, we have used cat states (pixel art of cats), various pixel art, audio, MIDI, DNA sequences and protein amino acid sequences.
items.author: Daniel Bultrini

items.title: Entanglement and information dynamics in charged dual-unitary circuits with impurities
items.summary: Local parts of a closed, non-equilibrium quantum many-body system can reach stationarity through the buildup of entanglement between different regions. In this paper we investigate how this process is affected by the presence of a quantum impurity that breaks a global symmetry of the bulk. In particular, we study a charged dual-unitary quantum circuit perturbed by a symmetry-breaking, non-dual-unitary gate acting on a spatially fixed pair of sites. In this setup we calculate the entanglement entropy for a subsystem that does not contain the impurity, as well as the mutual information and logarithmic negativity for a bipartite subsystem that straddles the impurity. We obtain exact results in the early time regime for these quantities from the dual unitarity of the bulk system. Beyond this regime, we compute the predictions of the quasiparticle and entanglement membrane pictures, supporting them with exact calculations obtained by taking the corresponding limits of the bulk entangling power. We find that the presence of a symmetry-breaking impurity can lead to a richer behaviour of quantum relaxation, including non-monotonic evolution of the entanglement entropy, a modification of the long-time steady state, and persistent subsystem mutual information and entanglement negativity. This behaviour is understood in terms of long-range correlations generated by scattering from the impurity, and facilitated by the ballistic propagation of the conserved charges.
items.author: Shachar Fraenkel, Colin Rylands

items.title: Hankel determinant for a perturbed Laguerre weight with pole singularities and generalized Painlevé $$\text {III}^{\prime }$$ equation
items.author: Shulin Lyu, Yuanfei Lyu

items.title: A Charge-Consistent Long-Range Machine-Learned Interatomic Potential Compatible with Quantum Linear System Algorithms
items.summary: Abstract Charge equilibration in machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) requires repeatedly solving linear systems, providing a promising target for quantum linear-system algorithms (QLSAs). However, conventional electronegativity equalization schemes suffer from spurious fractional charges between neutral fragments at large separations. To address this limitation, we incorporate atom-condensed Kohn–Sham density functional theory approximated to second order (ACKS2) into a long-range equivariant neural-network MLIP. Across benchmark systems, the ACKS2-based model improves energy, force, and charge predictions. At a molecule–metal interface, ACKS2 restores molecular fragments to near-neutral charge states upon separation while preserving local charge redistribution near adsorption. Because ACKS2 charge equilibration reduces to solving a linear system, the classical solver can be directly replaced with the Harrow–Hassidim–Lloyd algorithm during inference, demonstrating compatibility with quantum linear-system solvers. These results indicate that ACKS2 provides a promising framework for charge-aware MLIPs and highlight a potential pathway toward atomistic simulations based on QLSAs.
