items.title: The hidden symmetry operators of the asymmetric quantum Rabi model and its two-photon and two-mode variants in closed form
items.summary: The asymmetric quantum Rabi model, a two-level system with splitting $Δ$ and bias $ε$ coupled with strength $g$ to a boson mode, has level crossings when $ε$ is an integer multiple $N$ of the mode frequency. They are due to a hidden symmetry operator $J$, for which no general formula has been available. Here we obtain $J$ in closed form for every $N$. We find that $J$ is given by the parity of the symmetric model times the continuant (ordered tridiagonal determinant) of $N$ first-order operators, which are the Hamiltonians at the intermediate biases $N-1,N-3,\dots,1-N$ minus a common number operator. The symmetry is thus a staircase of $N$ bias steps that closes on the mirror image of the model precisely at integer bias. The proof uses induction on two commutation relations. The same relations hold in the asymmetric two-photon and two-mode models, written with the generators of $\mathfrak{su}(1,1)$, so that the same continuant gives their symmetry operators for every order, previously known only for the lowest ones. We also relate the closed formula for $J$ to the known recursion relations for its coefficients and give their terms of lowest order in $Δ$ explicitly.
items.author: Marcus Kollar, Arka Dutta

items.title: Enhancing valley splitting in Si/SiGe Wiggle Well quantum dots through integrated stressor-gate architectures
items.summary: Engineering large and reproducible valley splittings is essential for the scalable operation of silicon spin qubits. In Si/SiGe quantum dot devices, valley splitting arises predominantly from atomic-scale disorder and is therefore inherently random, motivating approaches that introduce a large deterministic contribution. Strain-assisted Wiggle Wells provide a route to deterministic valley splitting by combining an oscillatory Ge concentration in the Si well with shear strain; however, generating the required strain in a manner compatible with large-scale architectures remains a challenge. Here, we propose patterned stressed thin films as a scalable approach for generating shear strain in the quantum well of Si/SiGe quantum dot devices. Finite-element simulations show that compressively stressed TiN films can generate shear strains exceeding 0.1\% at the quantum well, sufficient for deterministic valley splittings of hundreds of $μ\text{eV}$ in strain-assisted Wiggle Wells. We show that this strain can extend across multiple quantum dots and is maintained in realistic gate geometries, providing a fabrication-compatible approach for scaling deterministic valley splitting to quantum dot arrays.
items.author: E. S. Joseph, Talise Oh, D. E. Savage, D. S. Stone et al.

items.title: Property F implies weak integrality for non-degenerate pivotal braided fusion categories
items.summary: We prove that every non-degenerate pivotal braided fusion category with property F is pseudo-unitary and weakly integral. In particular, every modular category with property F is weakly integral. Neither sphericality nor pseudo-unitarity is assumed. Passing to the Drinfeld centre extends the result to degenerate categories whose dimensions are positive on the intersection of the Müger centre with the adjoint subcategory; these include every braided fusion category with a pseudo-unitary Galois conjugate. Physically, the result connects the arithmetic of topological orders to the computational power of anyon braiding: non-integer squared total quantum dimension guarantees infinite braid group images, a necessary condition for universal quantum computation.
items.author: Justin Asher, Jonah Berean-Dutcher, Clay Cordova, Julio Parra-Martinez et al.

items.title: GARI++: A General-Purpose Decoder for Quantum Error Correction
items.summary: We present GARI++, a two-stage decoding pipeline achieving accuracy competitive with the state of the art across surface, bivariate bicycle and color codes without relying on ensembles. The first stage uses GARI, a normalized min-sum decoder with random serial scheduling on the GARI transformed matrix. The second stage decoder is used only for the cases that the first stage does not converge, and the decoder is configurable based on the choice of the QEC code. The first stage pipelines towards the second stage both the residual syndrome and the soft information. GARI++ pipelining is predictive, meaning that GARI++ chooses the first stage iteration outputs which are expected to deliver the best accuracy in the second stage. GARI++ motivates a hybrid FPGA-CPU architecture for real-time decoding. For example, under uniform circuit-level depolarising noise with a physical error rate of 0.001, the FPGA implementation of GARI achieves average latencies per round ranging from $201 ns$ to $11.8μs$ for surface code distances between 7 and 25. At the same time, due to the very low weight residuals output by the first stage, the average residual decoding time per round remains near constant and below one microsecond on a single Apple M2 core for surface code distances even up to 51 when using Union-Find and accuracy on par with correlated MWPM.
items.author: Arshpreet Singh Maan, Francisco Garcia-Herrero, Daniel Bascones, Valentin Savin et al.

items.title: A short proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture via the completion framework
items.summary: We give a short proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture. If a partial Boolean function $f$ is defined on a $δ$-fraction of all $n$-bit strings and have quantum query complexity $Q(f)$, then, for every $0<ε<1$, a deterministic algorithm computes $f$ correctly on at least a $1-ε$ fraction of its domain using $O( Q(f)^6 / (εδ)^2)$ queries. Our proof uses the completion framework and establishes a more general bound in terms of the classical adversary measure. The only result we use from Turturean's recent proof is a special case of his certificate inequality, for which we provide a self-contained proof. We also derive the stronger variant of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture, the bounded-polynomial influence conjecture, from our main result in the appendix.
items.author: Thomas Huffstutler, David Miloschewsky, Supartha Podder

items.title: Quantum Simulation of Quantum Channels and Applications
items.summary: We review the basic theory of quantum channels and develop a strategy for simulating them on digital quantum computers, drawing upon the \emph{Choi-Kraus operator-sum representation} and Stinespring dilation to provide a unified approach for various applications. We discuss three types of applications, offering explicit examples for each: the preparation of mixed states, measurements described by positive operator-valued measures (POVMs), and the simulation of the evolution of Markovian quantum systems. We recover fundamental concepts from quantum theory, such as the purification of a mixed state and the Naimark dilation associated with a POVM. Regarding the simulation of the evolution of a Markovian quantum system, we introduce an operator, termed the residual operator, to construct, from the system's Liouvillian, a quantum channel that serves as a first-order approximation of the quantum dynamical semigroup. This allows the simulation of quantum dynamics to be performed in a manner analogous to the Euler method for ordinary differential equations, avoiding Trotterization. We prove all the theoretical results mentioned, with the exception of the fundamental Choi-Kraus theorem concerning the operator-sum representation of quantum channels, for which we provide the appropriate references. The explicit simulations discussed were implemented using the AerSimulator from IBM's Qiskit SDK, with the corresponding code available on GitHub.
items.author: Lúcio S. Fassarella

items.title: Universal semiclassical drift velocity of magnetic edge channels
items.summary: Magnetic edge channels, arising at the edge of a two-dimensional electron gas in a magnetic field, are topologically protected and propagate unidirectionally along the edge. Their group velocities at the Fermi level, being averaged harmonically, result in drift velocity, which is related to the edge density of states, quantum capacitance, and the velocity of edge magnetoplasmons. Using semiclassical quantization of electron skipping orbits, we show that the drift velocity equals 1/2 of the electron Fermi velocity in the limit of a large number of edge channels crossing the Fermi level. This result, being universal for a hard edge and for isotropic dispersion, is checked numerically for massive electrons and for massless electrons in graphene. The drift velocity at smooth electrostatically defined edges lacks such universality. In the case of anisotropic dispersion, the semiclassical drift velocity at the hard edge reduces to a coordinate-velocity correlation along the cyclotron orbit.
items.author: Ekaterina R. Sleptsova, Alexey A. Sokolik

items.title: Self-Energy Construction for Chain Representations of Open Quantum Systems
items.summary: We identify the self-energy as the environmental response to the system, which transforms covariantly under shifts of the system--environment cut. For a semi-infinite chain with asymptotically uniform parameters, this transformation admits a fixed point that defines the asymptotic boundary self-energy (BSE), whose spectral density is the Wigner semicircle. A chain-extended BSE exploits the trend of the retained chain, offering improved accuracy in representing the environment. The transformation introduces a pseudo-hyperbolic self-energy distance that is invariant under shifts of the cut, providing a natural geometry for comparing environmental responses. As a demonstration, this geometry enables cut-independent error measure of finite damped-oscillator closures of the chain, distinguishing the closure error from the chain depth error, and offers a more accurate fitting scheme than fitting the time-domain correlation function.
items.author: Pengju Chen, Da-Wei Luo, Ting Yu

items.title: Unified architecture for arbitrary two-qubit gates with neutral atoms
items.summary: We propose a unified architecture for two-qubit gates in neutral-atom quantum processors which allows the implementation of the complete set of two-qubit gates. Our approach rests on a single resource that unlocks the entire gate set: an XXZ interaction with tunable anisotropy, combined only with single-qubit operations. We introduce a Rydberg-atom realization of the tunable XXZ interaction and combine it with optimally controlled global microwave pulses to implement the B, QFT, iSWAP, and $\sqrt{\mathrm{iSWAP}}$ gates, as well as a continuous gate family interpolating from CZ to iSWAP via the B gate. This work allows the implementation of any two-qubit gate natively in neutral-atom platforms, enabling flexible switching between instruction sets to reduce circuit depth and compilation overhead in quantum algorithm implementation.
items.author: Nader Mostaan, Peter Schmelcher, Rick Mukherjee

items.title: Curvature equations coupling symmetric tensors with a metric
items.summary: There are described hierarchies of equations coupling a metric with a trace-free tensor having prescribed symmetries and in the kernel of certain generalized gradients. These specialize, when the tensor vanishes identically, to the usual hierarchy of constant sectional curvature (projectively flat), Einstein, and constant scalar curvature. At the Ricci curvature level these equations are formal analogues of the Einstein-Maxwell and supergravity equations that couple differential forms with a metric. The particular cases coupling a metric with trace-free symmetric tensors satisfying the Codazzi or conformal Killing equations are studied in detail. Examples of solutions are obtained from mean curvature zero immersions, affine spheres, isoparametric hypersurfaces, and related algebraic constructions. The formalism yields a hierarchy of curvature equations for statistical structures. There are deduced constraints on the scalar curvature of the metric occurring in a solution that generalize classical results of Simons, for mean curvature zero hypersurfaces in spheres, and of Calabi, for hyperbolic affine spheres.
items.author: Daniel J. F. Fox

items.title: Catastrophic failure of quantum annealing owing to non-stoquastic Hamiltonian and its avoidance by decoherence
items.summary: Abstract Quantum annealing (QA) is a promising method for solving combinatorial optimization problems whose solutions are embedded into a ground state of the Ising Hamiltonian. This method employs two types of Hamiltonians, namely a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian. After a sufficiently slow change from the driver Hamiltonian to the problem Hamiltonian, the target ground state that corresponds to the solution can be obtained. The inclusion of non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is believed to enhance the efficiency of the QA. Meanwhile, decoherence is regarded as one of the main obstacles for QA. This paper presents examples to show that non- stoquastic Hamiltonians can lead to catastrophic failure of QA, whereas a certain decoherence process can be adopted to avoid such failure. More specifically, when anti-ferromagnetic interactions (i.e., typical non-stoquastic terms) are included in the Hamiltonian, the target ground state cannot be prepared even with an infinitely long annealing time for some specific cases. In the example presented herein, owing to a symmetry, the Hamiltonian is block-diagonalized, and a crossing occurs during the QA, which leads to a complete failure of the ground-state search. Moreover, it is shown that adding a certain type of decoherence can yield the ground state after QA for these cases. This is because, even when a symmetry exists in isolated quantum systems, the environment breaks the symmetry. In summary, the counter-intuitive results presented herein provide an insight into the fundamental mechanism of QA.
items.author: Takashi Imoto, Yuichiro Matsuzaki

items.title: The Geometric Deformation of Curved $L_\infty$ Algebras and Lie Algebroids
items.summary: While $L_\infty$ algebras are fundamental structures in differential geometry and mathematical physics, the geometric information encoded in such structures is often implicit. We address the following question: What constitutes a geometrically meaningful deformation of an $L_\infty$ algebra arising from vector bundles, and how can such deformations classify new geometric invariants? Inspired by nonabelian extension theory of Lie algebras, we define geometric deformations of curved $L_\infty$ algebras constructed from a vector bundle $V\to M$, and demonstrate that such deformations uniquely correspond to Lie algebroid structures on $V$. Explicit computations reveal that a representative of the first Atiyah-Chern class is exact in the total Weil complex, with its primitive representing the modular class in Lie algebroid cohomology. In the case of action Lie algebroids, the leading-order Atiyah-Chern classes correspond to the equivariant Chern characters. Applications to BV theories show that the geometric deformations naturally generate Poisson sigma models. These results provide a coherent framework for deriving field theories from geometric deformations of $L_\infty$ algebras.
items.source: Symmetry Integrability and Geometry Methods and Applications
items.author: Xiaoyi Cui

items.title: Generating interesting scientific ideas using knowledge graphs and LLMs: Evaluations with 100 research group leaders
items.summary: The rapid growth of scientific literature makes it increasingly challenging for researchers to identify novel and impactful ideas, especially across disciplines. Modern AI systems offer new opportunities for scientific ideation, but how compelling are AI-generated ideas, and how can their quality be improved? Here, we introduce SCIMUSE , which generates personalized research ideas using a knowledge graph of 58 million papers and a large language model (LLM). A central focus of this work is to understand how interesting these ideas are. Therefore, we conducted a large-scale evaluation in which more than 100 research group leaders—spanning the natural sciences to the humanities—rated over 4,400 personalized ideas according to their level of interest. Overall, expert ratings were modest (mean 2.40 on a 5-point scale, most common rating 1), while 24.9% of ideas were rated 4 or 5. We find that supplying concept pairs selected using the knowledge graph does not improve expert-rated interest over a titles-only GPT baseline. High-citation-predicted pairs even showed a weak tendency (1.94 σ ) toward lower interest than random pairs. Nevertheless, graph features can be used to control properties of ideas, and, using this unique evaluation dataset, we show that idea interest can be predicted with both a supervised neural network based on graph features and a zero-shot ranking approach based on an LLM. Our work provides an AI methodology for generating scientific ideas and a large-scale interdisciplinary expert evaluation, paving the way to study and improve difficult-to-measure metrics such as expert-perceived scientific interestingness.
items.source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
items.author: Xuemei Gu, Mario Krenn

items.title: Sequential decoding of the XYZ 2 hexagonal stabilizer code
items.summary: Quantum error correction requires accurate and efficient decoding to optimally suppress errors in the encoded information. For concatenated codes, where one code is embedded within another, optimal decoding can be achieved using a message-passing algorithm that sends conditional error probabilities from the lower-level code to a higher-level decoder. In this work, we study the XYZ$^2$ topological stabilizer code, defined on a honeycomb lattice, and use the fact that it can be viewed as a concatenation of a [[2, 1, 1]] phase-flip parity check code and the surface code with $YZZY$ stabilizers, to decode the syndrome information in two steps. We use this sequential decoding scheme to correct errors on data qubits, as well as measurement errors, under various biased error models using both a maximum-likelihood decoder (MLD) and more efficient matching-based decoders. For depolarizing noise we find that the sequential matching decoder gives a threshold of 18.3%, close to optimal, as a consequence of a favorable, effectively biased, error model on the upper-level YZZY code. For phase-biased noise on data qubits, at a bias $η= \frac{p_z}{p_x+p_y} = 10$, we find that a belief-matching-based decoder reaches thresholds of 24.1%, compared to 28.6% for the MLD. With measurement errors the thresholds are reduced to 3.4% and 4.3%, for depolarizing and biased noise respectively, using the belief-matching decoder. This demonstrates that the XYZ$^2$ code has thresholds that are competitive with other codes tailored to biased noise. The results also showcase two approaches to taking advantage of concatenated codes: 1) tailoring the upper-level code to the effective noise profile of the decoded lower-level code, and 2) making use of an upper-level decoder that can utilize the local inform
items.author: Basudha Srivastava, Yinzi Xiao, Anton Frisk Kockum, Ben Criger et al.

items.title: SimPoly: Simulation of polymers with machine learning force fields derived from first principles
items.summary: Polymers are a versatile class of materials with widespread industrial applications. Advanced computational tools could revolutionize their design, but the complex, multi-scale nature of polymers poses significant modeling challenges. Classical force fields often lack the accuracy and transferability that polymers demand, while quantum-chemical methods are prohibitively expensive for the large systems and long timescales involved. Here we develop a fast, scalable machine learning force field and show that, trained on quantum-chemical calculations alone, without any experimental data, it predicts measured bulk properties across a broad range of polymers. It reproduces polymer densities as accurately as, or better than, established classical force fields and captures the glass transition signature in the density-temperature curve, enabling the prediction of glass transition temperatures. To accelerate progress in this domain, we release a benchmark of experimental bulk properties for 130 polymers and an accompanying quantum-chemical dataset, laying the foundation for a fully in silico design pipeline for next-generation polymeric materials. The authors develop a machine learning force field trained only on quantum-chemical data that can reproduce measured key polymer properties such as densities and glass transition temperatures.
items.author: Gregor N. C. Simm, Jean Hélie, Hannes Schulz, Yicheng Chen et al.

items.title: Investigating production of TeV-scale muons in extensive air shower at 2400 m underground
items.summary: Abstract Deep underground experiments present a new avenue to probe the first interactions in extensive air showers or hadronic interactions in the extreme forward phase space. The China Jinping Underground Laboratory, characterized by a vertical rock overburden of 2400 m, provides an exceptionally effective shield against cosmic muons with energies below 3 TeV. The surviving high-energy muons, produced in the first interactions of extensive air showers, open a unique observational window into primary cosmic rays from tens of TeV up to the PeV scale and beyond. This distinctive feature also enables detailed studies of charged hadron production in the earliest stages of shower development. Using 1,338.6 live days of data collected with a one-ton prototype detector for the Jinping Neutrino Experiment, we measured the underground muon flux originating from air showers. The results show discrepancies of about 40% corresponding to significances of more than 2 $$\sigma $$ σ , relative to predictions from several leading hadronic interaction models. We interpret these findings from two complementary perspectives: (i) by adopting the expected cosmic-ray spectra, we constrain the modeling of the first hadronic interactions in air showers and provide novel insights into resolving the long-standing muon puzzle ; and (ii) by assuming specific hadronic interaction models, we infer the mass composition of cosmic rays, and our data favor a lighter component in the corresponding energy range. Our study demonstrates the potential of deep underground laboratories to provide new experimental insights into air shower physics and cosmic rays.
items.author: Xinshun Zhang, Shaomin Chen, Wei Dou, Haoyang Fu et al.

items.title: Phase dynamics of self-accelerating Bose-Einstein condensates
items.summary: Self-accelerating Airy matter waves offer a clean setting to access the intrinsic cubic-in-time phase. Here we reconstruct the relative phase of simulated Airy-shaped Bose-Einstein condensates from interference fringes in free space, a regime approached in microgravity. The cubic phase dynamics are quantified via approximately debiased, windowed polynomial fits with systematics-aware uncertainty estimates that account for window-induced correlations. We compare two physically feasible phase-extraction methods, heterodyne-based and density-based, and show that an Airy-Gaussian geometry yields substantially improved robustness to fit-window selection relative to an Airy-Airy collision. In the weakly interacting regime, the extracted cubic coefficient responds linearly to leading order to the effective interaction strength, its shift from the noninteracting value providing a calibrated probe of weak mean-field nonlinearities in self-accelerating condensates.
items.author: Maximilian L. D. D. Pellner, Georgi Gary Rozenman

items.title: Constraints on redshift-evolving Hubble constant models with early- and late-time diagnostics
items.author: Yupeng Yang

items.title: Registration Epistemics Finite Embedded Observers, Quotient Measurement, and the Limits of Self-Certification
items.summary: A finite observer can be genuinely adequate to a declared task; what it cannot obtain from the same current interface is a final certificate that its registration exhausts every task-relevant finer distinction. This paper develops the framework behind that claim by separating three levels that earlier versions partially conflated. P0 states the constitutive structure of realised distinction: a distinction requires first-term uptake, maintenance across a comparison span, and the independent resolution of a second term; these are not three interchangeable resources but three irreducible aspects of one distinction-making act. P1 states that their physical realisation in any current observer is finite and non-zero; P2 states that every resource actually used in that realisation belongs to the embedded observer. The number two therefore enters before Shannon: one anchor can register presence, whereas two are the minimum arity of a non-trivial relation and first permit same/different and, for live succession, before/after. Measurement is consequently quotient formation rather than cost-free read-out. We distinguish six quotienting mechanisms and isolate a physical self-referential limit based on generative-grain / resolving-grain asymmetry: full-grain current self-resolution cannot be implemented at the same current registration grain. The same minimal relational structure constitutes registered temporal order without purporting to derive substrate time. Epistemically, the framework separates theoretical awareness, instance adjudication, and final certification; it is non-sceptical because refinement can correct earlier blindness even though no current finite interface thereby acquires a final certificate of exhaustive grain. Two domain-general corollaries follow: every regis
items.author: Ruipeng Shi

items.title: Deterministic Language Model Phenotype Identification via Non-Lexical Multi-Manifold Topology, Semantic Information Geometry, and Inverse Gumbel Watermark Forensics
items.summary: Scientific monograph and technical architecture specification presenting a dictionary-free, non-lexical mathematical framework for generative language model (LLM) phenotype identification and statistical inversion of Aaronson Gumbel-Max cryptographic watermarks. The framework replaces vulnerable surface-level lexical heuristics (such as perplexity, burstiness, and n-gram overlap) with phase-space invariants derived from differential geometry, dynamical systems, and information physics:- Phase-space attractor reconstruction via Takens delay embedding theorem and correlation dimension D2 estimation.- Discrete Ollivier-Ricci curvature computed across semantic neighborhood graphs using optimal transport (Wasserstein W1 distance).- Quantum information geometry formalisms, including density operators rho, quantum state purity gamma, von Neumann entropy, and the Peres-Horodecki positive partial transpose (PPT) entanglement test.- Regularized 7-dimensional Mahalanobis distance with Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage covariance calibration evaluated against an empirical null-hypothesis (H0) baseline.- Blind forensic inversion of pseudo-random Gumbel-Max selections through inverse CDF transformations and Galois Field GF(p) residue coincidence testing. The system demonstrates robust resilience against false-positive errors on formal legal, patent, and mathematical prose. Its computational complexity permits real-time document analysis in under 15 milliseconds in-memory (CPU-only), requiring zero GPU acceleration. Empirically validated across an automated test suite of 633 implementation tests across 78 packages and 239 mathematical verification tests.
items.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.author: Tobiasz Włoch

items.title: Electron-Induced Formation of C 2 on Si(100) from Acetylene and Ethylene
items.summary: Abstract Hydrogen Desorption Lithography on Si(100) demonstrates the ability of the Scanning Tunneling Microscope (STM) to create functional atomic-scale structures and devices. The dehydrogenation of adsorbed molecules represents a potential complementary technique that has received little attention. For example, formation of C2 could introduce local strain or act as a center for subsequent reactions and would inform positionally controlled mechanosynthesis, an approach with vast potential in surface patterning and functionalization. Here, we studied the electron-induced dehydrogenation of acetylene and ethylene on Si(100) at 4 K using STM. Excitation of acetylene at ≥+3.2 V induces configurational switching, including to a new sublayer-bonded geometry previously predicted to be an adsorption precursor, as well as migration and desorption. Excitation also induces dehydrogenation to C2. Switching between three observed C2 configurations can be induced by excitation at ≥+4.2 V. Simulations using density functional theory reproduced the experimental images based on the choice of functional, dimer-buckling averaging, and the inclusion of diffuse basis functions. In addition, dehydrogenation could be induced using field-emitted electrons on a scale ranging from a single molecule to a radius of >10 nm. These observations highlight the potential of carbon dehydrogenation as an additional tool in Atomically Precise Fabrication (APF).
items.source: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
items.author: Oliver MacLean, Marc Savoie, Damian G. Allis, Rafik Addou et al.

items.title: Roles of polarization and detuning in the noise-induced relaxation dynamics of atomic-molecular bose condensates
items.author: Avinaba Mukherjee, Raka Dasgupta

items.title: Divide-and-Conquer Simulation of Open Quantum Systems
items.summary: One of the promises of quantum computing is to simulate physical systems efficiently. However, simulation of open quantum systems remains challenging, as their evolution involves non-unitary operators. The Stinespring dilation can simulate an open dynamic using a logarithmic number of auxiliary qubits, but requires a high circuit depth, which is impractical for NISQ devices. An alternative approach is parallel probabilistic block-encoding methods, such as the Sz.-Nagy and Singular Value Decomposition dilations. These methods implement the action of a single Kraus operator on quantum hardware and require one auxiliary qubit for each operator. They also result in shallower circuits but are hybrid methods, and do not simulate the complete quantum dynamic on the quantum computer. In this work, we describe a divide-and-conquer strategy to combine the output of each Kraus operator dilation and obtain the complete dynamic on quantum hardware with a lower circuit depth. We also introduce a balanced strategy that groups the Kraus operators into an expanded operator, leading to a trade-off between circuit depth, CNOT count, and number of qubits. We perform a computational analysis to demonstrate the advantages of the method and present a simulation of the Fenna-Matthews-Olson dynamic on current hardware.
items.author: Thiago Melo D. Azevedo, Caio Leão, Pedro Linck Maciel, Adenilton José da Silva et al.

items.title: Optimizing the Ground State Energy of the Three-Dimensional Magnetic Dirichlet Laplacian with Constant Magnetic Field
items.summary: Abstract This paper concerns the shape optimization problem of minimizing the ground state energy of the magnetic Dirichlet Laplacian with constant magnetic field among three-dimensional domains of fixed volume. In contrast to the two-dimensional case, a generalized “magnetic” Faber–Krahn inequality does not hold and minimizers cannot be balls when the magnetic field is turned on. An analysis of the problem among cylindrical domains reveals geometric constraints for general minimizers. In particular, minimizers must elongate with a certain rate along the direction of the magnetic field as the field strength increases. In addition to the theoretical analysis, we present numerical minimizers which confirm this prediction and give rise to further conjectures.
items.author: Matthias Baur

items.title: Ultra-high precision speckle spectrometer enabling radio-frequency scale resolution of atomic spectra
items.summary: Abstract Laser speckle, the granular intensity pattern arising from random optical interference, provides a high-dimensional encoding of spectral information that can be exploited for precision metrology. Speckle-based spectrometers have advanced rapidly owing to their compact footprint, mechanical robustness and alignment agnostic nature, yet their spectral resolution has remained limited to the picometre scale. In this work, we break this limit by employing an integrating sphere as a multiply scattering cavity with access to a high range of path lengths to enhance spectral sensitivity. At 780 nm, the resulting device achieves a resolution of 6 fm, corresponding to a resolving power of 1.3 × 10 8 , representing an approximately 80-fold improvement over previous implementations. This ultra-high resolution enables clear discrimination of laser sidebands generated by an electro-optical modulator, with extracted sideband powers agreeing with expected values to within 1%. It further permits a direct speckle-based measurement of the hyperfine structure of the D 2 transition in 85 Rb, with transmission spectra differing by no more than 3.7% from independent wavemeter-referenced measurements. These results establish speckle as a platform for ultra-high precision spectroscopy, radio-frequency spectrometry, and microwave photonics.
items.author: Gabriel Britto Monteiro, Christopher Perrella, Sarah K. Scholten, Morgan Facchin et al.

items.title: Geometry of tangent bundles of statistical manifolds equipped with Cheeger–Gromoll type metrics
items.author: E. Peyghan, Leila Nourmohammadifar, Ion Mihai

items.title: Memory-like effects and kinematics of trajectories in cyclotron motion
items.author: Manthan Kashyap Datta, Mantra Mehta, S R Das

items.title: Quantum Dot Colloidosomes as Triggerable Microlasers
items.summary: Abstract Quantum dot (QD) supraparticle lasers are promising platforms for microscale light sources and photonic labeling, yet their optical properties are set during assembly. Here, we introduce QD colloidosomes, liquid-core/solid-shell supraparticles that combine whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) optical feedback with stimulus-triggered structural collapse. Intact QD colloidosomes exhibit narrow, cavity-defined emission consistent with WGM-assisted lasing from 4.2 mJ/cm2, with line widths of 2.2–3.7 nm, demonstrating light confinement without a solid core. We identify shell continuity as a critical determinant for WGM feedback and lasing by exploring a morphological continuum of suprastructures comprising solid supraparticles, colloidosomes, and microporous hollow shells. Intact colloidosomes support narrow cavity modes, whereas porous shells remain broadband even at high pump fluence. We show that colloidosomes can be driven to rupture and release payload through well-defined pathways, including meniscus-driven capillary failure, uniform heating, and localized near-infrared activation, thereby configuring their optical response from cavity-defined lasing to broadband emission. These results establish QD colloidosomes as stimuli-responsive microlasers that couple optical-state switching and triggered release within a single self-assembled platform.
items.author: Cristian Gonzalez, Saranya Subramanian, Marco Reale, Giuseppe Soligno et al.

items.title: Adaptive error management for fault-tolerant quantum computing across hardware-level suppression, system-level diagnosis, and real-time decoding
items.summary: Abstract Fault-tolerant quantum computing reached a milestone in December 2024 when Google’s Willow processor demonstrated below-threshold error correction on a superconducting chip, a result since reproduced on neutral-atom and alternative superconducting platforms. Yet the classical decoders needed to sustain this performance face a scaling challenge: noise becomes increasingly structured and correlated as systems grow, while decoders must respond within microsecond coherence windows. This survey asks whether error suppression, noise diagnosis, and decoding are better treated as one adaptive control problem than as three separate research programs. Drawing on a scoping review of 146 records, it organizes the field into a three-layer taxonomy. Layer 1 (Hardware-Level Suppression) integrates protection into the physical substrate; bosonic cat qubits exponentially suppress bit-flip errors, projecting up to 90% overhead reduction versus surface codes. Layer 2 (Diagnosis) employs probabilistic models and computational intelligence to characterize error sources; neuro-fuzzy architectures and the Bias–Entropy decomposition separate hardware drift from logical faults, subject to an identifiability limit that we characterize. Layer 3 (Real-time Decoding) targets the integration of machine learning within strict latency constraints. Hardware acceleration now approaches superconducting cycle times, which shifts the case for learned decoders from speed toward accuracy under correlated noise; recent advances favor hybrid, physics-informed architectures: Neural Belief Propagation resolves degeneracy issues in quantum low-density parity-check codes by embedding topological constraints directly into the network’s loss function. These results suggest a transition toward closed-loop AI
items.author: Marwa R. Donkol, Naima Kaabouch

items.title: Cross-regional hydro-meteorological cascade propagation modeling and emergency response optimization using temporal fusion transformer and spatio-temporal GNN
items.summary: Cross-regional hydro-meteorological disasters (e.g., floods, heavy rainfall-triggered cascades) often trigger cascading propagation effects with strong spatiotemporal dependencies due to geographical proximity, infrastructure interconnectivity, and socioeconomic coupling. Existing emergency response systems lack high-precision, interpretable predictive capabilities for such dynamic transmission processes, leading to delayed coordinated responses. To address this issue, this paper constructs a joint modeling framework integrating Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) and Spatio-Temporal GNN (ST-GNN). This framework inputs multi-source covariates from each region into the variable selection network of TFT. After gated residual processing, long-term dependencies are jointly modeled using multi-head self-attention and causal convolution, outputting regional temporal states. Simultaneously, ST-GNN constructs a task-adapted dynamic adjacency graph based on a predefined geographical adjacency matrix and adaptively learned edge weights. At each time step, neighbor nodes are aggregated and embedded, and node representations are updated via a time-gated mechanism. Both approaches align timestamps and concatenate features in each prediction step, generating risk intensity and prediction intervals through quantile regression. These are then used as constraint inputs for integer programming to solve resource scheduling schemes, forming a closed-loop decision. Comparative experiments show that this method achieves an average RMSE of 0.071 in the cascading propagation prediction of highly disturbed disaster distributions, a recall rate of 0.97, precision at 0.95, and an F1 score of 0.96 under extreme node network density, and an average response time of only 5.6 s under 500 nodes. items.author: Jonathan Washburn

items.title: Discrete Gravitational Field in the ZEBTS Framework: Canonical Construction, Convergence, and Reproducible Examples
items.summary: This paper develops a discrete gravitational framework within the ZEBTS axiomatic system and rigorously connects it to the modular ZEBTS‑SUPER program. We construct gravity as an emergent phenomenon of a discrete topological background, spectral objects (flytrons), and controlled topological invariants. Key results include: (i) a discrete Poisson equation on graph Laplacians with explicit control over gauge choices and solution uniqueness; (ii) a quantitative stability and error analysis grounded in the condition number of the Laplacian on the subspace orthogonal to constants, linking numerical robustness directly to graph connectivity and topological properties; (iii) computational checks on a four‑vertex chain graph that verify convergence rates, perturbation bounds, and force computations; (iv) a systematic closure of gap F3 of the ZEBTS‑SUPER program by demonstrating geometric consistency, including the reproduction of continuum limits and the structural role of flytron modes; (v) the embedding of spectral constructions (F1) and topological diagnostics (F5) as foundational elements of the discrete model. We further outline the immediate next step: the derivation of a discrete Weitzenböck identity and the establishment of equivalence with a Yang‑Mills formulation via the adjoint‑valued field χ, which will solidify the unification of gravity and gauge interactions in the ZEBTS framework. The approach yields not only a numerically stable discrete theory but also a self‑diagnosing model where topological invariants serve as explicit control parameters for convergence and stability. The results are supported by linear‑format formulas suitable for direct implementation and by a minimal Python‑style verification script, ensuring reproducibility and integration into the ZEB
items.author: Anatolii Mukha

items.title: Gravitational dressing: from the crossed product to more general algebraic and mathematical structure
items.summary: A bstract The crossed product, and consequent transition from von Neumann algebras of type III to II, is recovered from a truncation of more general gravitational dressing constructions, about certain spacetimes. This is done by extending “standard dressing” constructions previously used to give a perturbative definition of “gravitational splittings”, defining approximate localization of information. This result appears to illustrate that this algebraic transition is a small piece of a more general algebraic, or other mathematical, structure associated with quantum gravity. The leading-order structure involves noncommutativity from separated regions, and at the nonperturbative level connects with a possible explanation of holographic behavior for gravity.
items.author: Steven B. Giddings

items.title: Polariton XY-simulators revisited
items.summary: Introduction: Arrays of bosonic condensates of exciton–polaritons have emerged as a promising platform for simulating classical XY-models, capable of rapidly reaching phase-locked states that may be mapped to arrays of two-dimensional classical spins. The relation between the collective spatial modes and minimization of the corresponding XY-Hamiltonian requires clarification. Materials and methods: Here, we develop an analytical model based on the overlap matrix of individual condensate wavefunctions, its nearest-neighbor approximation, and reservoir-fed rate equations. Results: The model gives collective spatial configurations for chains, triangular lattices, and perturbed graphs. The triangular-lattice minimum changes between ferromagnetic (FM) and frustrated antiferromagnetic (AFM) order with the outflow wavevector. Near threshold, the normalized growth rates depend on pump overlap and mode losses. The small-array simulations illustrate the development of intensity patterns over 100 ps. Conclusions: The model relates spatial interference in polariton lattices to XY-type phase configurations and identifies how the pump geometry enters the condensation threshold. It provides a basis for studying the dynamics of mode selection.
items.author: Junhui Cao, D. Novokreschenov, Alexey Vitalievich Kavokin

items.title: Conserved quantities enable the quantum Mpemba effect in weakly open systems
items.summary: Observation of the quantum Mpemba effect has spurred much interest in its enabling conditions and its relation to the classical counterpart. Here, we consider weakly open many-body quantum systems initialized in different thermal states and examine when the initially farther state relaxes to the (non-equilibrium) steady state faster. We claim that the number of conserved quantities in the unitary part plays a crucial role: the Mpemba effect is possible only when the Hamiltonian commutes with other extensive operators or is integrable. The reason lies in the dynamical evolution happening in spaces of different dimensions. When energy is the only approximately conserved quantity, dissipation pushes the dynamics within a single-parameter manifold of different thermal states. In contrast, for Hamiltonians with several conserved quantities, the dynamics drift in the multi-dimensional space of generalized Gibbs ensembles, whose distance to the steady state is less trivial. We provide numerical results for large system sizes using tensor networks and free-fermion techniques, thereby supporting our claim.
items.author: Iris Ulčakar, Rustem Sharipov, Gianluca Lagnese, Zala Lenarčič

items.title: Interplay of orbital degeneracy and vacancies in stabilizing collinear magnetic order in Cr 1 + δ Te 2
items.summary: Cr$_{1+δ}$Te$_2$, a two-dimensional van der Waals ferromagnet, displays a contested magnetic structure, poised between collinear and non-collinear spin configurations. In this work, we investigate the magnetic structure of Cr$_{1.33}$Te$_2$ at the microscopic level by combining single-crystal neutron diffraction, X-ray absorption spectroscopy, and first-principles calculations. Neutron diffraction measurements reveal a distinct collinear spin alignment, whereas spectroscopic analyses reveal inherent structural vacancies at both Cr and Te sites. These vacancies lead to local symmetry breaking that elevates the orbital degeneracy of the Cr 3$d$ states, as demonstrated by our first-principles analysis. The resulting modification of magnetocrystalline anisotropy emerges as the key mechanism stabilising the collinear magnetic ground state over the non-collinear one in the presence of vacancies. Our findings uncover a vacancy-driven route to control spin anisotropy and magnetic ordering in layered ferromagnets, offering new insights into the design of tunable 2D magnetic materials.
items.author: Prasanta Chowdhury, Jyotirmoy Sau, Sourav Chowdhury, Dr Matthias Gutmann et al.

items.title: Robust valley splitting against interface atomic disorder towards scalable silicon quantum computing: Computational design
items.summary: Regardless of various material design strategies, experimentally achieving substantial and controllable valley splitting in Si/SiGe quantum wells remains a central challenge for ensuring high gate uniformity. This difficulty arises from unavoidable atomic-scale disorder at the interface, caused by alloy randomness, which suppresses valley splitting and, more critically, induces large variations. Here, we demonstrate that CMOS-compatible uniaxial strain can substantially enhance valley splitting, rendering it immune to interface disorder. Atomistic pseudopotential calculations show that uniaxial strain linearly restores the valley splitting suppressed by interfacial disorder, with a large enhancement rate, while keeping disorder-induced variations within a narrow distribution. We reveal that uniaxial strain introduces a new coupling channel between bulk valleys in adjacent Brillouin zones through a small momentum transfer, which markedly reduces the susceptibility of valley splitting to interfacial disorder. These findings establish a viable route to improve gate uniformity in silicon-based spin qubits, paving the way for scalable quantum processors.
items.author: Yang Liu, Gang Wang, Shan Guan, Jun-Wei Luo et al.

items.title: Stabilizer-based quantum simulation of fermion dynamics with local qubit encodings
items.summary: Simulating the dynamical properties of large-scale many-fermion systems is a longstanding goal of quantum chemistry, material science and condensed matter. Local fermion-to-qubit encodings have opened a new path for practical fermionic simulations on digital quantum hardware where fermionic statistics are not enforced at the hardware level. In this paper, we explore these local encodings from the perspective of the corresponding time-evolution unitaries. Specifically, we propose a new framework for digital implementations of these qubit-encoded fermionic time-evolution unitaries based on \emph{flow sets}, which are one-dimensional subsets of the directed fermionic interaction graph. We find that any local fermionic encoding, when restricted to a given flow set, adopts a simple structure that we can classify systematically. For each categorized flow-set form, we propose a low-depth qubit quantum circuit that implements the time evolution unitary using the stabilizer formalism. As an application of our construction, we introduce novel flow-based decompositions for known two-dimensional encodings, leading to efficient circuit decompositions of time-evolution unitaries. We generally observe a space-time trade-off, where mappings with larger qubit-to-fermion ratios yield shallower time-evolution quantum circuits.
items.author: Anthony Gandon, Samuele Piccinelli, Max Rossmannek, Francesco Tacchino et al.

items.title: Quantgraph: A receding-horizon quantum graph solver
items.summary: Dynamic programming is a cornerstone of graph-based optimization. While effective, it scales unfavorably with problem size. In this work, we present QuantGraph, a two-stage quantum-enhanced framework that casts local and global graph-optimization problems as quantum searches over discrete trajectory spaces. The solver is designed to operate efficiently by first finding a sequence of locally optimal transitions in the graph (local stage), without considering full trajectories. The accumulated cost of these transitions acts as a threshold that prunes the search space (up to 60% reduction for certain examples). The subsequent global stage, based on this threshold, refines the solution. Both stages utilize variants of the Grover-adaptive-search algorithm. To achieve scalability and robustness, we draw on principles from control theory and embed QuantGraph's global stage within a receding-horizon model-predictive-control scheme. This classical layer stabilizes and guides the quantum search, improving precision and reducing computational burden. In practice, the resulting closed-loop system exhibits robust behavior and lower overall complexity. Notably, for a fixed query budget, QuantGraph attains a 2x increase in control-discretization precision while still benefiting from Grover-search's inherent quadratic speedup compared to classical methods.
items.author: Pranav Vaidhyanathan, Aristotelis Papatheodorou, David R. M. Arvidsson-Shukur, Mark T. Mitchison et al.

items.title: Optimizing quantum state transformation under locality constraint
items.summary: In this paper, we present a general numerical framework for both deterministic and probabilistic quantum state transformations, under locality constraints. For a given arbitrary bipartite initial state and a desired bipartite target state, we construct an optimized local quantum channel that transforms the initial state into the target state with high fidelity. To achieve this goal, local quantum channels are parametrized on a complex Stiefel manifold and optimized using gradient-based methods. We demonstrate that this approach significantly enhances entanglement distillation for weakly entangled states via two complementary strategies: optimized local state transformation and probabilistic local transformation. These results establish our method as a powerful and versatile tool for a broad class of quantum information processing tasks.
items.author: Sasan Sarbishegi, Maryam Sadat Mirkamali

items.title: FTCircuitBench: A Benchmark Suite for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Compilation and Architecture
items.summary: Realizing large-scale quantum advantage is expected to require quantum error correction (QEC), making the compilation and optimization of logical operations a critical area of research. Logical computation imposes distinct constraints and operational paradigms that differ from those of the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) regime, motivating the continued evolution of compilation tools. Given the complexity of this emerging stack, where factors such as gate decomposition precision and computational models must be co-designed, standardized benchmarks and toolkits are valuable for evaluating progress. To support this need, we introduce FTCircuitBench, which serves as: (1) a benchmark suite of impactful quantum algorithms, featuring pre-compiled instances in both Clifford+T and Pauli Based Computation models; (2) a modular end-to-end pipeline allowing users to compile and decompose algorithms for various fault-tolerant architectures, supporting both prebuilt and custom optimization passes; and (3) a toolkit for evaluating the impact of algorithms and optimization across the full compilation stack, providing detailed numerical analysis at each stage. FTCircuitBench is fully open-sourced and maintained on GitHub.
items.author: Adrian Harkness, Shuwen Kan, Chenxu Liu, Meng Wang et al.

items.title: Gravitational form factors of the proton in the improved holographic QCD model
items.summary: A bstract We compute the gluonic contribution to the gravitational form factors of the proton using the improved holographic QCD model, in which the proton is described in terms of bulk Dirac fermions. Model parameters are constrained using lattice and phenomenological input, allowing us to obtain estimates for the gravitational form factors and to compare them with results from other approaches. Using the extracted form factors, we analyze mechanical properties of the proton, including pressure and shear distributions. We obtain estimates for the mechanical and mass radii of the proton, ρ mech ≈ 0 . 63 fm, ρ mass ≈ 0 . 65 fm, and compare these values with radius estimates from other nonperturbative studies.
items.author: Antti Hippeläinen, Niko Jokela, Matti Järvinen

items.title: New Solutions to the $$G_2$$ Hull-Strominger System Via Torus Fibrations Over K3 Orbifolds
items.summary: Abstract Using torus fibrations over K3 orbisurfaces, we construct new smooth solutions to the $$G_2$$ G 2 Hull–Strominger system. These manifolds arise as total spaces of principal $$T^3$$ T 3 (orbi)bundles over singular K3 surfaces. Our construction is based on the choice of three divisors on a singular K3 surface that are primitive with respect to a particular Kähler metric. The stable bundle is obtained via an adaptation of the Serre construction to the singular setting.
items.author: Anna Fino, Gueo Grantcharov, Jose Medel

items.title: Semi-device-independent self-testing of bipartite pure quantum states without nonlocality
items.summary: It has been known that all bipartite pure quantum states can be certified by quantum self-testing, i.e., any such states can be pinned down completely based on the statistics produced by local quantum measurements. A notable feature of quantum self-testing is that the conclusions remain reliable even when the quantum measurements involved are untrusted, where quantum nonlocality is crucial. This necessitates that each party conducts at least two different quantum measurements to produce the desired correlation. Here, we prove that when the underlying Hilbert space dimension is known beforehand, which is very common in quantum experiments, an arbitrary $d\times d$ bipartite pure state can be certified completely (up to local unitaries) by a certain correlation generated with a single measurement setting on each party, where each measurement yields only $2d$ or even $d+1$ outcomes. We also prove the robustness of our protocols to quantum noises and experimental imperfections. Compared with quantum self-testing, our protocols do not hinge on quantum nonlocality and are much more efficient, yet they maintain the essential feature of not requiring additional assumptions about the quantum devices involved. This advancement could offer significant convenience when certifying bipartite quantum states using untrusted quantum devices in future quantum industries.
items.author: Lijinzhi Lin, Zhenyu Chen, Xiaodie Lin, Zhaohui Wei

items.title: All you need is Trotter
